div.head: OUR CHRISTMAS CORNER.
div.p: OUR CHRISTMAS CORNER.

BY POVERTY-NOOK INTO FyRTHEft STRAITS. A MIGRATION OF THE WOODCOCK. k BY JOHN PEERS. "By lingering memories of fermer joys imPelled," and favoured by the happy conjunction of glorious weather and the Jubilee holidays, I formed the pro- ject of , revisiting, by means a one of mit hied boats, the scene of former delights, the Menai Straits. It was only after long and anxious &lib& ation. that it was decided to undertake the adven- ture, which we knew required the three essentiale of success—viz time, judgment, and pluck. Of these three raw materials of success the time helci the same'properrtions to the others thet Jack Fal- staff's " intolerable deal of sack" did to his "one half-pennyworth of, bread." And it is,the want oI thiselement, more than all the others, that prevente a more general following of this course as a summe holiday. It is too extended a trip for those wh are bound to be home again in a limited andi Axe time. and are thus prevented from awaiting, in patient dalliance, upon the caprices of the Weather:, the mariner's mistress, whose whims and fancies an 4 I ever changing, moods he must watch with a jealouk eye, and trim his sails, and regulate his outgoing, 1 and his incomings therewith. - Well. the auspicious moment came at last! Wif the Jubilee came what has been , called queen' weather, so we took old Time by the forelock once more—that tuft which has been so much pulled a this last three thousand years, and which he would have lost entirely but for the eonstant use ot Pomade Devine Doubtless carping critics might suggest that this is slightly antedated. To this I reply—" that it is a good argument in favour of Professor Snipeaad's Wide-world Periwig Restorer ,',' for had Father Time but known of this famous Repilatory (.N.B.—Barber.s may have use of this mint- new word by paying Royalty) he would have tamed his youthful locks up to now. Be this as it may, we did seize it, and good use we made of it. Shakespeare tells us somewhere—Or was it Job? quotation, are getting so 'very much mixed-110w— Luther is scarcely to he distinguished from which. No, on consideration. I think it was the divine Wil- liam, and not the exemplar* of patience, who said "there is a tide in the affairs of men which, taken at the fl od, leads on to fortune." Now the same may be said of the ebb—it was that which led us on to where "Taxes cease from troubling, and credi- tors are at rest." This came about the week before the Jubilee. Now, I strongly object to seeing other folks doing foolish things -7-not that I consider it an infringement of the monopoly —but from a possible feeling that it is the one "touch of nature that makes the whole world kin," and reminds me of Dr. Watts'—isn't it ?—who said, "For he is but a sample of what I might be." And so I foresaw no plea- sure in being a witnese of thia 'Jubilee disturbance. To see little children enjoy themselves upon any innocent pretext is pleasant enough, but to soe their elders trying to feign a joy they cannot feel i s very melancholy spectacle. Personally, I Can see no callgo for jubilation in the humiliating fact that for a space of fifty years at least a so-called self-goverwclpeople had subjected them- selves submissively, to the thraldom of a sham govern- ment, unadulterated royalty, and a diluted democracy. Our limited monarchy may be a rassible substitute for a better article 90 long as we are blessed by the reign of n Sovereign content to do so without entertaining or ex- hibiting troublesome ideas of meddling in politic*. That is, the nearer to the similitude of a dummy the Sovereign becomes, so much nearer does he attain to the ideal of a limited monarch. ' And plenty such can be stipplied on short notice and at reasonable rates by any Bond-street tailor. As what is wanted is merely a signing and assen- ting automaton, unswayed by inconvenient notions of personal government, some of our ingenious mechanic- ians might, for the good of their country, invent one, on the plan of the Automaton Chess-player, and maintain it in working order at very light expense ; thus affecting, in economy alone, a great saving as compared with the expensive and dangerous system nowin use. The Prime Minister might be entrusted with the key, and be respon- sible for the proper working and winding of His Majesty. Nor is it difficult to imagine all the other functions of royalty being performed by its spring impelled substi- tute, except its two most prominent and permanent ones, —the depletion of the Exchequer and the repletion of the Nursery. But this defect—is it to be imputed as a fault ?—might be got over by the employment of sub- stitutes to do the work, which! the Court itself would furnish in plenty, without taxing the energies of the people. A copy of the "Court Journal" of these days to come would be a curiosity, could we get one. There we should read not so much of what Majesty did; but what was done to His Majesty. Thus—" The Prime Minister had an interview with, His Majesty this morn- ing. The right hon. gentleman having duly wound up His Majesty, received the signature and Royal assent to the Rill for the Prevention of Pension List Peculation. His Royal Highness was then conducted into the Private Packing Case and locked up by the right hon. gentle- man." Now the danger I have alluded to consists in the very unnatural, and consequently very unstable nature of the system. Being composed of two sections—two elements —the so-called subjects' the actually governing section, and the so-calledmonarch,the actually governed. SO to speak, the affinities of this combination are extremely weak, and it is liable to fly asunder when sufficient fric- tion oeeurs. An active democracy dominated by a mon- arch, is in the condition of a loaded gun, ready for the direst mischief when the cap (of liberty) is meddled with. Whenever we in England have the unhappiness to lose the present mild oocupant of the throne and have, the unspeakable misfortune to suffer the accession of a monarch possessed of intellect and a strong will, with the inclination to intermeddle in party politics, we shall soon be in the position to regret not having set our house in order by the quiet process of deliberate legislation ; far "prevention is better than cure." But throw polities to the dogs; wo are on holiday thoughts intent. With the obvious exception of a little extra preparation and providing, our outfit was much as usual in our frequent trips down the river. Nor was the voyage down to Rock Ferry embellished by adventure worthy of record. Past the curiously associated names of Dungeort and Poverty Nook, we soon arrived at our destination. But allow me to introduce to the notice of my readers our ship, the Woodcock, 20 feet over all, 16 feet keel. 7ft. ein.beam,.draught 20 inches, increased at will to sft. by means of a centre board. Our crew, hearts of oak of ceurse, consisted at first of the skipper, to whose abundant kindness and perennial generosity we were indebted for the loan of the boat. Then sinnm Simon, the Vulcan of this aquatic Olympus, minus his Venus though, whom special mission it would seem tab* to find a place for eyerythingandtoput everything in its place, in whose abseice the boat quickly becomes an odd assortment of sixes and seven's. Then not last, if least, comes Alf, lithe and limber, who has no equal as cook's mate's minister, the Skimmer of the broth, the deft re- triever of hidden requirements from the lumber encum- bered recesses of the dark forepeak. But at length, full length, and at last, Comes Jack, of whom perhaps. the least said the better, for are not his favourite failings and fatuities " writ large" in these pages? In accordance with previous arrangement, we put into New Ferry, and landed the skipper and his mate Simon.. and took aboardamong other good th ings a passenger boutid for the West.. With a mutual wave of the hand, we round the boat outinto the strong ebb tide then running, and are soon swept by it through the crowded Sloyne Into the narrower and ever-turbulent waters between Liverpool and Birkenhead. Past new Brighton and into the Rock Channel as the light began to fell us, over the tail Of the Dove Spit to find the tido spent, and tho narrow road into Hoylake one tangled maze of rippling shoals and meandering shallow. Too late! And the night coming on! The sun had merged his glory in the western sea, and the polestars were one by one asserting their right to shine. The light northerly breeze fluctua- ted, faltered, and ultimately died away. This, combined with the smoothness of the sea, just slightly heaving with the pulsing throb of the landward breeze ren- dered our enforced stay not at, all unpleasant. There was no help for it, we were shut out and must "bide a wee." If a patient submission to the inevitable be philosophy—then were we lovers of /risdom. We tifrned our thoughts inwards and found how very hollow we were, and so set about supplying this long-felt want. After a little rest and refreshment we had the young tide making, which soon enabled us to seek in the lake a less exposed and less isolated position. L.mong the weird- dimlyseen forms of the great fishing craft, we wended our devious way to a berth opposite the light-houses. Here we at once proceeded to "snug down" and make up for past deficiencies of rest and sleep. • (To be contimird)

A BIT OF CHRISTMAS. "Where are you going to, my pretty maid?" "To gather some Christmas, sir," she said. "And what is some Christmas,' my pretty maid ? " '44 Holly and mistletoe, sir," she said. "May I go with you, my pretty maid?" " Oh yes, if you don't mind the snow. sir," she said: "May I carry your Christmas' now, pretty maid ?" Well, yes, I suppose, sir," she smiled and said. But he carried the mistletoe over her head, And soon like the holly her cheeks were red. And as through the village they shyly sped, "A fine bit of Christmas," the gossips said: From" Yule Tide."

div.head: SNOW AN' NICE.
div.p: SNOW AN' NICE.

Our Kitty is a tall of snow— As round, as soft, and just as chilly— And, when for "sentiment" you go, She coldly smiles and thinks it "silly." Fier ways are quiet and demure, And gentleness is all about her; And strife is stiller, life more pure And sweet than it would be without her.

And greatest cold and greatest heat, They tell u.s are in close alliance: Then would your coldness melt, my sweet, Were I to set it at defiance ? She sees the love-light in my face, With less of scorn my hopes she's pelting, I take her in my warm embrace-- I do believe the snow is melting! From "Hood's Comic Annual."

MY AUNT'S STRATAGEM; OR, THE TWO GHOSTS. BY J. Stamm One evening in the month of January, 18—, I found myself seated around the cheerful fireside of my dear old uncle and aunt's cottage, standing some few miles on the outskirts of Manchester. In answer to a long- standing promise I was spending my New Year's holidays with them, and certainly no one could bay.. receiv;el a more genial welcome than did I when I put my bead in at the door some few days before the opening of my story, and wished them all "a happy new year." "Eh. bless mi, if it isno' eawr navvy Jack !" was the joyful exclamation of my uncle John, who had opened the door. "Come forrud, lad, an' let's see heaw theaw art !" and the good old man led me by the hand to the kitchen, where a bright fire burned merrily, casting dancing shadows upon the pictures which adorned the In her rocking chair sat my aunt, a portly, good- looking dame, who rose upon my appearance, and, with hands extended, exclaimed: "Well, aw never! an' so theaw's managt t' find thi way here at last, haste, Jack? Wotever's kept thi away so lung, Jack? Ccoartire, aw reckon (looking slyly at me), same us o th' rest o' yung lads I blushed violently at the " soft impeachment," for had I not left behind me the sweetest and fairest girl in Manchester—or so she was to me? So that my aunt had hit remarkably near the truth. Such had been the manner of my reception, and as each day passed they both strove to make my visit as enjoyable as possible. The evening on which I introduce myself to the reader ' was the eve of my departure to my employment—that of a clerk in a certain warehouse situate not far from Market-streets Messre.Stubble & Green having graciously granted me a few days' holiday, owing to my having given up a portion of my summer holidays to relieve the pressure of business which just then chanced to be very brisk. After tea my uncle' aunt, and I drew our chairs around the fire, prepared to spend the night in social intercourse, in winch reminiscences of past events would no doubt come in for a large share. "Aunt," said I, "tell me how you and uncle there first got to love each other, will you?' My aunt smiled lovingly at uncle, and after a pause said: "Well, Jack, aw think aw will, just to pleeus thi, but theaw munno' say nowt 'tit aw've done, wilta?" I gave the desired promise, for on a previous visit I hed tried to get my aunt to tell me her love-story, but could not succeed in doing so. "Well, Jack, when aw're a wench aw're considered to hi very pretty' bi mi faythor an' mother; an' aw mun say ut when aw placed misel aford th' lookire-gla.ss, ut aw thowt ut they wurnt far wrung. Like o' country wenches, a liket bein praised, mooar so when th' praise coom fro' yung men. "Neaw, thur wur two Tung chaps ut uset to follow me abeewt, eych one tryin to get afore th' other. As sure as aw geet eawtside o'th' dur aw're sure t' be met bi th' two chaps—Jim o Jones's an' Bill o' Chips they wur coed. A* cud see they hated eych other like peyson; but when wi' me they purtended t' be as civil an' as pleasant as they knowed heaw. Heather Jim or Bill dust come within twenty yards ut th' heawse,'for mi fayther 'ud ha pullet urn booath away, for he wur gradely feed o' losin mi just then. Aw cared for noather on urn, for a thowt mooar o' another's little finger (glancing lovingly at my uncle), than a did o' booath on urn put t'gether. "Booath Jim an' Bill bad t' pass th' churchyard t' get anywheer oar place wheer they wur likely t' meet mi' and fro' wot aw yerd, they'rn awfully feeart o' pasain through th' churchyard when Fooin whoam ut neet. Booath on 'ens ud towd mi ot different times ut nowt but th' the w% o' havin a few words wi me 'ud mak um brave enol' t' run t' risk o' tumblin o'er a ghost or a i goblin n th' churchyard. Knowin heaw feart they wur aw made up mi mind t' play um booath a thrick—one ut ud freeten em so mich ut they'd stop a wboam for th' time t' come. Aw purtended to Jim ut aw liket him betther then Bill, an' towd him ut aw wish Bill ud stop ruunin after nti. 'Neaw, Jim,' said aw, one day when aw're wi him. Awl' tell thi o' a plan ut'll freetin him away., an' leeuv the road clear for thi.'" "Jim wur rare an' pleaust at this, but his face cleawded o'er when aw towd him wot aw wanted him t' do; an' that wur get a sheet an goo in th' churchyard on a sartin neet menshuned by me, an' wi th' sheet o'er him, freeten Bill back, an' he met bi sure he'd noan come agen. Jim wur as big a coward as here an' Weer one, hut th' thowt o scoria' a victory o'er Bill deter- Mined Jim t' try th' plan. "Th' followin neet Bill met mi, an aw tuk care t' give him a gradely gpel welcome. Bill seamd rayther sup- prised at th' way aw resaved him. " Heaw is Jim o' Jones's gettin on, Bill?' aw axt him in a sperrit o' mischief. ' aan ye' parted company or "• Aw no nowt abeawt him, an' care less,' wur I surly reply. He's a meun, snakin rascot, that's what I be is, an aw'Ye towd him ut th' next time aw catch him comm ether thee aw'd put his yed reet off his shoodherse " "'Eh, bless mi life an' cowl Bill,' aye cried, theaw'd never do sich a thing as that, surely?' "Alw'd do mooar than that for thy sake, Sarah,' said Biil, an' he lookt at mi same as a lad some times looks at a happo' when he sees it eawt o' his reych in a shop windy. " • Aw'm geetin sick an' teyrt o' that Jim o' Jones's doggin mi abeawt,' aw sed, 'an' aw think aw con plan summut us'll bi betther then puncin Jim's yed off.' ' "' Wot is that?' said Bill. "Then aw towd him us aw'd towd Jim, ut he're t'. bi in th' churchyard wi a sheet o'er him, at th' same time as aw'd towd Jim he're t' meet Bill; noather on urn, us yo seen, knowin ut th' other wur t' bi theer." "And did your plot succeed, aunt ?" I asked, eagerly. "Wait a bit, Jack an' theau 11 see," was her reply. Fro' wot aw yerd after it seeums ut Jim geet one o' th' *sheets off his bed, an' rowlin it up. seet off to th' church- yard, his yed filled wi dismal fancies o' ghosts an' other unarthly things. As Jim enthert th' churchyard his yure begun a liftin his cap, an' he thowt he cud see a aperrit every shadow ut th' moon throwed on th' graves abeawt. A cat ut darted past him made Jim give a skrike, an' made him drop beheend a gravestone as if he'd bin shot. Here he stopt till his friset had partly gone away fro' him. Tremblin i' every limb Jim pre- pared t' cover hissel in th' sheet, an' havin done so stretched hissel full length beheend th' stone so as t' bi ready for Bill, when he should come past on his way to meet me. e Bill had also gPtten a sheet, an' abeawt th' time ut Jim had planted hissel beheend th' gravestone, climbed o'er churchyard waw, which was but a low one, Bill geet beheend a stone; but this not suitin' him, he're preparin t' find another hidin place, when suddenly he yard a footstep. Welly freetent to th' deeath, Bill stud stock still for a minit or so, when he seed summut white comin up t' him. Wi a yell o' fear Bill tarns to his heels. I th' other 'ghost' doin th' same, but in th' opposite direckshun. Booath on urn, it seems, geet fast in thur sheets. an' rowled o'er an' o'er, eych thinkin one wur fallowin' th' other. Rushin whoam, booath on um said they'd seen a ghost in th' churchyard, an' no matther scot th' owcl folks said, nowt ud convince um (Jim' and '1) but wet they'd seed wur rayley an' truly wot they Bis hice,ved it to bi. Booath lads geet a gradely freet, so ut they kept thur beds for a wick. Aw didno' limas n think 0, ,;-arryin th' joke so far, but it wur done, an' so couldno bthelpt." "Did chiv:Arne again, aunt ?" said I. "That tyoidno. Whether thi uncle theer, geet wynt o' th' affair or not aw conno say; but vet,/ soon afther he aid mi if wed marry him, an' as soon as 'axins' wur o'er wi geet wed, and (smiling benigdly at my uncle, who Was Complacently smoking his ciiiurch- warden opposite) fro' that day to this errn nevdr had cause t' regret th' bargain." the night having now grown apace, I, after w:ishing in an affectionate "good night," left them with the that my married life in the bright future whlch lay me, Might be a's happy as theirs had proved to Bea Britrley's Journal.

Owd iron bahanged ! " aw see, " the're my skeets us aw paid noinepence fur threw seasons sin. lw rec- kon tins thowt o' makkin a gud thing eawt on urn; bur avrna. noane gooint be don eawt o' mi pleasure furt sake o' thi, germ. abeawt three pier:es o' rbblidn' stoan'i 1 fur urp." Hoo sad nowt, un th' chap went away', tin aw browt th' skeets i'llYheanserm begun riggin' urn up ready fur use. Avrd settlet mi naiad on a piece o' wayter I' Xoonleet-lone cawd th' Herrin' Pit, un after. lappm mi tackle up 1' one o' earn. Betty's linsty petticoats, aw seat off. Aw kept gooin same u. 61 iv a wur vralkin • fur a wage 4 whoile th' strings e' th' petticoat wur danglin' abeawt mi heels bike ribbins: Awto6k no notice o' what folk sed abeawt mibecose iv a-4- had aw shudn't a' gotten to th' far eend hi this. Aw reached th pit at last welly starvent to deeath, un after abeawt three-quarters oy an heawr's serewin', pooin, an' strainin' aw manisht furt fasten mi skeets'on. Aw geet on th' ice un went reawnd th' pit i' nil Owd style. There wur groom on th' pit besoide wissel, be- cose th' Herrin' Pit wur a gra,dely place fur skeetin' th' frosty weather, un yung folk ust come fro am parts o' th' world. Some o' th' cracks us irst come sed th' ice o' this pit wur th' best under th' moon. Awd a bit uv a rest, un aw thowt awd tak a short cut across th' middle toth other soide. When aw rag abeawt noine yards o', mi journey th' ice begun givin Way, un aw wur soon up to mi neck' ith nit. Everythin wur reaw aw confusion onth ice un folk wur tryin t' scams th' best plan furt got mi eawt. After a bit o' considera- tion, owd Jonty's plan wur browt into operation, un before aw cud speak ther wur a rope thrown reawnd mi neck un twenty pair a' honds pooin us hard as they: cud. Aw begun thinkin they wur aimin fart poo mi yead off,when a extra snatch londet rni on th top oth ice. Aw wur bike a bundle o' slutch, aw wur sich a mess; un after gerrin up omi feet owdJontygenmi sich a shalt- in us aw shant forget us long us- aw live. Aw pooed mi skeets off, un made th' best o' mi road whom. When aw geet insoide th' dur aw wangt th' skeets uppoth floor, un pooed aw ml gloothes off un went bed. APT towd eawr Betty hoo must wash th' does, becose aw shud want ' humfust thing ith' mornin after, as they wur aw aw , had. When aw wakkent mornin after, boo sed hood washt th' clops us aw sed, bur theyd run up so, they wurnt big enough fur eawr Jack, a lad o' seven year I owd. Aw wur bad i' bed mony a wick after this sufferin fro neuralgia i' mi leg, us th' doctor sed. Th' heawse wur welly full every Sunday mornin wi folk commn o' seem n heaw aw wur gerrin on, after mi dip ith Herrin Pit; until aw wur aw rest again. BILLY UT TH' GUIDE'S GOOSE. D'ye know Fit-broo- Billy ut th' Guide? He's a chap as hes lots o' good fnends. Theyre o scattered abeawt in a circle so wide,— Fro Haydock reight reawnd to t' Loyne,Ens. He con sten a fair nook in a spree. Un ut gaminin',wey, Billy's the lad! Bud ut cookin', he's gawmless a bit; dornd yo see, Aw've a tale neaw to tell yo o'er thad? Last Kesmaa to Earlestown he coom, Un wur soon agate raffia' wi' th' dice; In a tooathry minutes he'd qetten sum rum,— A quart bottle full, temptlnl un nice. Then he geet on wi' guessin' ut throws, Un won middlin' o' brass, beside booze, Then Billy, as o th' fooak reawnd th' "Blackamoor " knows, Shook, .un won a gret thirteen-peawnd goose! Tort hooam Billy trundled wi' th' prize, When id geet rayther late on ut neer, Un he clung to thad goose, for he meant to surprise His wife wi' thad glorious sea ! Hein' fuddled, his progress wur slow, Bud he reyched th' Guide, beawt moytherin' Un his sheawt wakkened up everybody i' th' row, " Gooa to Earlestown for champion geese!' Billy's wife heeard his din, un geet up, Lest him in, un he blobbered eayrt streyt, " Owd lass, reytch a glass un thast hey a good sup, For aw've getten six penn'orth o' meyt !" Theer he wur, balanced up ageon th' speer, One hand full o' goose, t' other—rum; Un he red as he put em on t' table, " Neaw, theigher ! Tha con see as owd Resmas hes come!' His wife stared, fairly wakkened, ut Bill, Un boo axed " wheer hes t' gotten these ?" Billy answered her "Betty, thee say wod tha will, Earlestown's t' shop for good ruin un big geese!" As he showed signs o' sleep, soon up stairs Hoo geet hur worn chap, snug i' bed. N. Bud Betty slept nooan, for boo thowt unawares, Till day bronak, o'er wod Billy had sed. A goose! Hoo'd ne'er cooked one in hur (Thinkin', allus a woman disturbs.) Bud when Billy geet up, he enleetened his wife, "Tha mun stuff id wi' bread crums un herbs! Rooast id i' th' oon, for th' dinner to-morn." Then Betty hur way 'gan to feel, "Will you herbs do, on t' shelf, as tha geet for Ovrd Thorn?" "Ay!' sad Billy, "they'll do Yana weel !" Kesmas day cootn, un dinner-time browt Th' goose on th' table, to Billy's gret glee; Then he flourished his knife un sad, "Betty, ther's nowt Aw like better than goose—except thee !" He cut hur a leg, took Vother hissel, Doled eewt Ptuffin' un gravy apiece. • Ut th' fost raeawthful he give sitch.a horrible yell, Bawlin "Help! help! Aw'm pizon'd—fotch t' pliee!" Nayburs rushed to see wod wur to do. Billy cut th' goose i' lumps, "Taste o' thad !" ' They tasted, then darted reawnd t' corner to spew, , Forth' goal flesh wur terrible bad. Billy's temper flew up,—he wur wild; Un he stampt abeawt, cossin' like mad; Betty's " Paddy " rooase too, un hoo skriked Th' dinner's spoiled, Tha ne'er brings nowt bud rubbish like thad!"

Wod things mut ha' goan to, n)bry knows, Iv Owd Thorn hedn'd nooatised t' big creawd, Un just stopt to inquire wodever wur th' cause As ther sturnmicks bed getten so preawd. He tasted o' t' goose,—th' stuflin' too, Then sed " Billy, thi heyd's like this jawm, This stuffin's t' wrong herbs,—Hey, tha hollow-brained foo! Newt bud wormwood, us yarro,un bawm!"

PARLOUR PASTIMES. THE BLIND MAN'S WAND. A'player is blindfolded and stationed it the centre of the room, a li.ght cane or wand being placed in his hand. The rest of the company join, bands, and, dance around him, singing the chorus of any popular dittv they please by way of enlivening the proceedings. Wien the last note is sung all stand still. The blind maa holds out his wand, and the person towards' whom it chances to point must, according to the rules of the game, take hold of the end. The blind man then gives three cries, which the player holding the wand must imitate as well as he can. If he fails to disguise his voice he is fcund out, and has to take the place of the blind man. If not, the players 'dance round as before. WHAT IS MY THOUGHT LIKE? Is a game requiring players with at fair allowance of . brains. They sit in a line, except one he stands "(rut" facing the others. This last writes down the name of the person or thing thought about, and then, without re- vealing what she has written, turns rapidly to any one of the players and demands, "What is rny,' thought. like?" An answer must be given before twenty is counted, and then the original "thought" is read out.-and the last speaker must prove the likeness between the two things. - Sometimes there is a ludicrous disparity, and the player is at her wits' end to find the smallest resemblance Be- tween the "thought" and what she has ignorantli de- clared it to be like. A funny story is told of Tom Hood, the poet and punster, and of the ingenious manner in Which he extri- cated himself from such a difficulty when playing "What is My thought like ?" with a distinguished

group. A lady asked the usual question, and Hood's answer was "A nunip." "Then," said she, "you will have to prove the re- semblance between a pump and Lord C—h, for thought of him:" and she showed the name of the noblt. man written on her paper. 'Every one was delighted, and wondered how even the prince of wits would proVe a resemblance between his lordship arid the pump. But after the briefest possible pause Hood said, "Lid C-11 is like a pump— Beesilso it is All 'awkward' thing of worst, Whicla up and ,lown its awkward arm doth sway. And spout. ag)a spout, and spout. :wad spout away. In one weak, waany. everlasting ,flood." The nobleman in question happened to be a weary speaker and ungaining in his appearance, and this reply was equally ingenious and apropos. A protty compliment was conveyed to a friend who had written "Time Cornet" as her thought, and asked a young gentleman player what it was like? lie answered. "'Foam-elf," and proved the resemblance in the following Bees, the lady having already rejected • many suitors You. like the oomet, holt' our eyes In thrall; Witere'eat yon ge attract the gaze of alt; And yet pursuit Is useless, for you teach That, like the comet, yon are out or reach. TWEITY QUESTIONS is a game which requires the players to be wide awake, because in answering the questions they must keep from saving I, no, yes, black, or white. Here is a specimen of the questions and answers. . What is the colour of your frock? Snow colour. As white as snow? More like milk. • Is my coat blank? You ought to know. What should you call it? A coat. I mean the odour? Soot colour. Can you give a direct answer? Judge for yourself. Have you any brothers? 'rwo. Do you love ihern? Very much. Do they love you? Ask them. Are you happy hers? Very. Have you lost an article of dress? Let me search my wardrobe tosascertain if one is missing. Is not this yours? (holding up a ragged pinafore). You know it is not. Your name is on it. Are you certain it is not yours? Tbo name is a forgery; the garment is not mine. What do b-l-a-(rlt spell? A word that must not be named by me. Is it true that you cannot spell words of two syllables? Try me. Will you write them down? Give me pencil ard paper ind you shall see. What do si-o spell? A word expressing negation. Will you pronounce it? When my twenty questions have been answered. How many have you answered? This makes twenty. And off bounds the witty girl amid the plaudits of these around without having incurred a forfeit. It is so very natural to say " no " and " yes " that few players escape without forfeits, and only theso who have their wits about them can successfully parry the rain of queries to which they are subjected. CHARADES AND PROVERBS IN TABLEAUX. Charades and proverbs in tableaux are acted, not spoken. The charade words must be divided into syllables, each one of which is represented in a tableau, end the whole word is given in a final tableau scen"e. Proverbs are given in one scene only. At the conclusion of the drama, the guessing begins on the part of tho audience. If they are successful, they, in their turn, perform, if not, they minas' as audience. A very pretty tableau can be made from the word "work," by repre- senting several trades, each at Osman bench or table. The blacksmith hammering a horse shoe, the dairy-maid making butter, the cobbler mending a shoe, the milliner trimming a bonnet. In short, as many figures as the size of this room will admit. The dresses may be as the players think best. Its acting a proverb, say, "A rolling stone gathers no moss," the player takes some- thing to represent a stone, and rolls it on the floor, then picks it up and inspects it, and appears dis- appointed. This is sepented, and the player must con- vey to the audience the Idea that he thinks the nakedness of the article that represents the stone very strange.* The following are a few words suitable for charades : Band-age, Hand-some, Watch-man, Purse-proud, Bride- cake. As for proverbs, almost any of the& will do, such as "A stitch in tune saves nine," "Take care of the pence and the pounds will take care of themselves," "Fine feathers make fine birds," &c. Charades may be acted. For dresses, blankets, shawls, &c., may be used. A screen should be hung across the end of the room. Impromptu charades are always the funniest. Here are a few words for charades :—Accent, Axe-sent; Hamlets Ham-let; announce, Ann-ounce; artful, art-full; apes( ape-x ; ka.

CHAPTER XV.. , A 'WEDDING rms. , ..s. , . , , Several days passed without further event. Anne ''Derrick went about her daily work in the farm-housi in her usual quiet, methedieal fiishion: After the supreme excitement she had gene through in th last fortnight,—into,whieli an age of acute and vatic emotions seemed to have been. compresged—thes days were to her afterwards likes a blank in her memory, and her over-strsined brain and nerves were fora tune numbed into torpor. Ohe thing indeed aroused in.her a :vivid anxiety-,-would the deformed girl write to her again, as she had half promised ti, . Mrs. Lawson went to Tavistock.ai usual on the market day, and again on Imi...return she gave Anne a letter. It was addreesed,in the same fernininb handwriting, and bore the 'Plymouth post-mark 01. before. "I cannot come to sre y;oungain," the defo ed. girl wrote, "as we are i just leaving Plymouth,. 'But it does not matter, as t ha.s all been cleared u about the dismond. MY friend lia.4 explained me that he lest it when he, was out hunting one da, . I shewedliim your advertisement, and he will w • to you himself." . . . Thus Abruptly ended thesnote. Would he write, that owner of the Missing link , 1 Anne very much doubted. it. , She bitterly regretted not having gone to Ply- mouth, on the desperate chance of being able to find the ,eirl whom she. had met by the riverside at ' Tavistock. In losing her, she had perhaps lost the only clue to the murderer, and yet how would it have been possible tss discever her in a large and thickly-populated town, when the only description she could give of the ,girl was that she was short,. pale, slender, and slightly deformed? Her only hope of finding her would have been through the police, and Anne shrank from doing this, as it would involve revealing he 'Who s was, and- what was her reason for seeking the gist.. She had abeliefmore unreasen- able than one would have expected from suet' a sensible womaa—that they would refuse to help her, for magistrates, police, and all the machinery of the law were banded together against Martin. It was a belief which had unconsciously grown in her ever since Martin's first. arrest after the death Of Dick Lawson, and which had been strengthened by the , long course of boycotting which she and her brother. had endured. "Everybody is against iss," she thought; " every- body in authority—everybody well-to-do and re- spectable. James Stanihridge has never been near me since. Susan's death—has never so much as sept me a letter or a .raessage." - , ! "I never had much opinion of Captain Stambridge ever since I lost my poor son' "said Mrs. Lawson, one day. She no longer shrank froth speaking openly to Anne •, , she knew, as Anne had told her again and again, that she was the only friend that Aune had in the place—she, the woman who had lost her only son through the act of Anne's own brother. . "Captain Stainbridge came to see me, to sympathiite with me in my trouble, he called it," Mrs. Lawson went on; "and because I wouldn:t Join in with what lie was saying, he as good as told nie I , was a poor, mean-spirited creature. So I says to ' him.—' When Job was in his affliction, there was a _foolish woman came and told him to curse God and die; and you're little better, Captain Stambridge, says I; for you want me, in my sore trouble to surse .4 good man; for a good man Martin Derrick is, whatever yOu and the folk hereabonts may say. And I know if he lives till he's fourscore, he'll ' sniffer in his mind every day of his life for what lie did in just one moment ; ana it may be as it's Only right and reesonable that he should ; but I'll not be the one to add by'a feather's weight to the burden he hag to bear. l'vly lad is in God's hands, and Martin Derrick is in God's. hands too, and He has mercy enough for them both.' " Souls filled with energy, high courage, faith—like Anne Derrick—can "subdue kingdoms and stop the month of lions "; :but there is an inheritance Of the earth for meek creature-s like Mrs. Lawson. This forlorn and -humble Widow Wielded a power given her by her sympathy, her perfect simplicity, and self-forgetfulness. . "What would be the use of my having been in such trouble if it, did not make me feel for you and your brother ?•' she said to Anne; and Anne could only marvel at her. ' • "If 1 bad hecn in Mrs. Ls.wson's place," she thought, "I could • never have been such • a :good- woman as she is." -.„.! . I' • "To go hack to what I WM saying about Captain Stambridge—" sail Mrs. Lawson, after a minute'a silence, while idle quietly shed a few tears--" Who is lie to talk because your brother can't bring forward anybody who met him on the moor that Friday even- ing? Where was Stanibridge himself, that's what I want to know? The woman as cooks and cleans up for him told me hergelf that lie was ont all that evening, end never got home till past eleven o',clbck at night, and he's one that comes home early to his supper in general. W here was he all those hours, that's the point, and why did nobody think: to ask him at the inquest ?" . " But study you don't think Captain Stambridge had anythinr, to do with—with the murder of my sister ?'l. asked Anne, startled. Until that moment she had :forgotten her own slight suspicions .of . Stambridge, so completely had her mind been filled with the vague, mysterious form of the man who had dropped the diamond in Martin's room. "No, I don't know as I do, Miss Derrick," the widow replied hesitatingly. "Only, if, as I say, he has got no witness to prove where he was that even- ing, why does lie condemn your brother ?" Anne hued planned anot.ier visit to Martin, when she would tell him all about the diamond sleeve-link, and her meeting with the deformed girl, and together they would consult upon the next steps to be taken.' She was arranging her daily affairs—her household, her dairy, and a certain amount of superintendence of the'ont-door work on the farm, which she felt to be one of her chief ditties in -Martin's absence—iklie was arranging how best to Secure a leisure day when she could go to Exeter, when she remembered one thing she had as yet 'omitted to do. She had intended to'make up some of Susan's clothes into parcels, to give away to the poorest women in the village. So she determined to do this at once. It was a painful, lint also a charitable task, w:cieli should no longer be delayed. She took down from a peg in the wardrobe in her sister's room, the black silk and cashmere gown which Susan smell to wear every day, which she WAS, wearing, in fact, when she was murdered. Amie shud- dered a little es she touched it, but she, forced hers: self to spread it out upon the bed, and to begin care- fully folding it up. There was, she knew, n the village of St. Stephen's, a poverty-stricken' i widow, mother of several little do-lighters, whom no super- stitious fears would hinder from tinning that gonei Into a girl's frock. As Anne Was folding it, she discovered that a tiny black silk bag was sewn into the lining ef the bodice. She touched it ; it felt as though it contained paper, and it was not an unlikely hidingpla,ce for a bank note. . ' Anne took a pair of scissors froni Susan's workbox and eut the stitches which fastened it to this bodies,. There were two folded papers inside the 'bag. One was a letter; as she opened it there dropped out of it a 'wedding *ring. The other paper was a certificate of marriage at a London church, between ' Francis Carteret and Susan Derrick. , The letter was addressed "My dearest Susan," and was signed, "Your devhted husband, Francis Carteret." . It was of a commonplace nature enough, but it was evi- dently written by a man of education, apparently e;ven a gentleman; it contained .no address) no clue to the whereabouts of the writer, but it,tosts dated, ' and the date proved it was written a few weeks after the marriage, and theiiertificate established that to -have taken place nearly eight years ago. ,Anne placed the papers, so strangely discovered, on the dressing-table, and sat down to try to think out the matter .clearly. She was half stunned by surprise; her brain whirled with a multitude of , thoughts, with tle rush of hope that here at last , she held in her hands the means of freeing Martin. How truly he had said, that they--the brother and Sister knew ' little of • Susan's - past life; and that they must look . there for the explanation sof the mystery which . over- shadowed her death. Who was this :Francis Carteret-f could he •be still living? And would susan have eared to commit bigamy by going through a form of marriage with Jame Stems bridge ? Of course, if Francis. Carteret were dead, the, whole care which Anne was 'constructing fell to the ground. Da supposing that Susan did not know for ecrtain whether Ye Was alive. or dead, then wnat an easy explanation tWat wmild be of her hesitation about marrying Stanibi:idsc, her varying moods, her caprices, her terror' 4310/, so inexpliCable at the time, %a perfectly to be uuderstood now', if she could not satisfy heraelf.,if Shewas legally free to marry again. -"--Ahd thenL4uppiisiag-Ifilisan's husband Lhad sud- denly -reappeared. But what whuld lie have to fear if she had married Stambridge ? On her would fall the Punishment. What nasild lia his

rnbtive for destroying heit unless, indeed be had: also wished to marry some one else. Then like. lightning came the thought—if he Was the man who owned the diamond sleerediuk, he was the man who was engaged— to- -marry • the girl whom :Anne had met under the _Map7 wails at Tavistock. At tlili4 point Anne seized thtletter and it through once more. lut. therepras no fact of any importance to be gained. from it,. except the date of the- year when it was written. "NOwi where was Snsan, then," pondered her Slater. "I remember irow, she was living at Mrs. Norton's, in one of th 4. cr,mennts at Bath. Yes, and it was near the end of Ora year that she came home SO suddenly, and looked so ill and miserable. Her husband' had deserted her by that time, no doubt. I. wonder if that Mrs. Non 13 stialiving in Bath, and whether if I scent to see her :she-could-tell meanything abont Susan whilst she was in her Service hick would throw any VA 'upon this marritLge. . It is a forlorn hope ; but, so i far as I can see, t is my only one at present.. . Oh, it is cruel ", she eXclaimed bitterly. "Why have, I been •so Vatfled, au& disqppointed ? Why d that girl escape me at TavistoCk? I might have found. out everything from her." (To be con-t yen'.)

,cp4sERVATITE. MEETING AT LATCH- . ' ' • MR. JOHN WHITE AND ALDERMAN • ' OROSFIELD.. A meeting of the Conservatives of Latchford Ward was held in St. James' Schoolroom, on Monday evening. Mr. John White presided, and amongst others on the platform were Mr. W. Touchstone (Manchester), Councillor J. Taylor, &c. There was a small attendance. A vote of condolence with Mrs. Reynolds on the death of her huslsind. Captain Reynolds, was passed, that gentleman, it being. men -- doped, having been chsirman of the Conservatives of Latchford Ward for upwards of 20 years— The CHAIRMAN, in the course of an address haying reference chiefly to Ireland, remarked that Mr. John Crosfield, in one of thosellashes of eloquence for which he was so famous', said there was something grander than law, and that was justice. Well, that sounded very well, but he was afraid it was not quite logical. Those of them who were familiar with Holy Writ knew that the. word judg- ment accompanied the word-justice--when justice was mentioned they almost invariably had judgment. With- out law they must have anarchy, and where they had anarchy they could have no justice. Speaking about Crosfield, he should like to take that opportunity of making a personal explanation, or, rather, not exactly an explanation, but a reply to some remarks Mr. Cro• s- told made at the hbkquis of Ripon's meeting at thePuh- lie Hall a few days ago. (Hear, hear.) He hardly- thought it necessary as a rule to reply to anything that Mr. Crosfield said, because he agreed with Mr. Murray in his letter to a local newspaper the previous week, is• which he said that Mr. Crosfield wispot a model of a thoughtful statesman. He might say that Mr. Cros- field's sayings could hardly be said to impress one by- their 'wisdom or logic, no were his sentences as rounded as those of a Demosthenes, while his eloquence was of a somewhat turgid description. (Laughter.) When ho get up to make a speech he generally reminded one of that famous passage of Gratiano in the "Merchant of Venice

*" lam Sir Oracle. , And when I ope my lips let no dog bark." (Laughter.) He (Mr, White) should not have alluded to that subject On his own account, but it had been pointed out to him that if he did not contradict the statement Mr. Crosfield had made it would injure a cause which he had so much at heart, that was the question of Fair Trade. (Applause.) Mr. White then read the following pa,ssage from Mr. Crosfield's speech—" He (Mr. Crosfield) dare say they were fond of Mr. John White, but he did not think they were fond enough to supporta duty on corn which would raise the price of a 41b. loaf by, Per' haps, 2d. The object of that fair trade cry was to raise the rents of farms, to put money in the landowners' pockets, and to raise the screw of the agent." (Laugh- ter.) If that meant anything it meant that he (gr• White) went to a meeting in Warrington for the purPoee of advocating a movement which was to benefit himself. There could be nothing more contemptible or more mean than for a man to take part in a political movement for the sole object of benefiting his own pocket. He did, not believe that Mr. OroSfield himself thought so ill him as to think he would do a thing of that kind, and if he (Mr. White) thought his townsmen of Warrington, thought he was guilty of such an action he should no', show his face on .a platform again. (Hear, hear.) Bd• as usual Mr. Crostield was talking about sometking he knew nothing about. He was, however, glad to sal' that Mr. Crosfield was correct in the fact which he noted that he was agent to several landowners in the neigh" bourhood. -He was very,proud of that connection was protid-to serve the men he did serve, men who had so much at/heart the interest of their tenantry and neigh' bours. But lie might state for the benefit of Mr. Cros" field that the landowners of this aountrypaid their agents by fixed salaries, and so far as he knew, those maaree„ Seldom or never altered. Although rents had bem goill6 down for the last few years he weal:glad:to say that hie salary remalped the same, and if rents were to go up l?; morrow 10s if, statute acre it would not make the difference to his salary. Mr. Crosfield was evideotif under the impression that land agents were paid 1317, commission, but that was entirely false, and it was onz: on a par with the arguments that the Radicals wer- in the habit of bringing forward at meetings. A committee and delegates to the eounv'''' were also appointed.--Mr. LEE proposed, and Mr. Golg; DING seconded a resolution supporting the Goverrone"„ in its Irish policyr—This was supported by an address or "Ireland and Home Rule," hy Mr. Touchstone, afte„, which the resolution was carried. . . 'CHAPTER 2Clt.—Eontintied. THE ii:E4TINGI Etlr THE ' RIVEIL Anne went down the sloping pathway to the river side. Her spirits were raised, her nerves were braced up .by. the t ope that she was about to find the key 'which would un:ack Martin's prison doer. The grey old ivalls Of the Abbey,' overhung. With thick growth of ivy, were on her right hand; on her leftitefzie itAni 'ivy, rushing swiftly over its rooky, bed, with little waves breaking against boulders, little cascade &ailing :into :pale light, which was just visible through tbe gloom, of that December evening, . Anne :went on steadily, wondering, whoni she was going to Meet. Would it be a thief, Who hoped to rob her of the diamond.? Would it be—a darker pos- sibility still—SuSan'S murderer, who would try to save his own life by destroying a witnemagainst bun Then from out the darkness suddenly moved ihtii the middle of the path confrontina; Anne, a site-: slender; feminine figure. "Are you Mrs. Lawson?' asked.a faltering, girlish voice: - • "That is the name I advertised by," replied relieved, yet disappointed—surely this hoped-for meeting would prove a miserable failure after all. Then she saw another woman standing against the wall, under the canopy of overhanging ivy. "That is only my maid, you need not mind speaking before her," said the girl, contizig a little closer to Anne.. There was just light enough for her to discern a young' pale face, with irregular features, and large eyes. She was very plain eertainly ; her figure was slightly deformed; and something in the wistful expression of her face teuelted Anne with pity. She was simply dressed in the, brown ulstei and felt hat which she had mentioned in her letter, but as she moved something andoienly flashed at her throat, and Anne, with almost a superstitions thrill, saw that the girl wore, ma brooch, a diamond set in plain gold, like the fatal:-e she had locked, up in her bureat at home. "I wrote you that letter," be;an the girl in slow voice, with a subdued hurry and excitement about her.. ?!. I wanted to see you—to ask you something about that diamond which von found. A friend of mine has lost one—at least I think he has, but I can't get him to tell me—or else be has given it away to some one. I must find Ont. Pleasc,'' she; implored, "tell me where you found it.".. Anne, though impressed by there being something simple and genuine abotib the trembling girl before her, yet remained upon her guard. "I could not bell you that, until' yen have first told me exactly what the diamond your friend has lost was like. Tell me how it was set, and what it was used for, and so on." "Oh, I'll tell you. I'll tell you everything," the girl answered eagerly. "It is. a sleeve link ; there are two diamonds in each one of the pair; they are set in a perfectly plain and rather heavy gold setting, and there is a little gold chain between each two of the diamonds, so as to form the sleeve link. I don't know 'whether I have expressed myself clearly enough. Is the diamond you have found one of them: Please tell me." ' "You have described it exactly," replied Anne. : She turned deadly cold, for a few moments sbe was unable to speak—then she became 'aware that the' girl was addressing her in great excitement. "Then tell me where you :found it, arnd what you. know about it. You must tell nie. You don't know how much depends upon it!" "That is just what I, do know," Anne replied, in a tone which' sounded' almost sarcastic. .put in her heart she was praying wildly--" Oh, Go]; give me- wisdom ! What shall I say to her—how much dare I tell her ? " . "You say you are not the owner of the dia- mond," Anne at last said slowly. " Then why do you ask me questions about it! Why don't you tell me who the owner is, as you say you know him ? " "I can't—Oh, I can't; he would never forgive me if he knew I had been trying to find out about it. It Would make matters much worse." "Thin, I am very sorry, but I can 'say nothing more. I have the diainoed that your friend has lost, that is pretty certain, and I ought to be told who the owner is." Here the other woman who had been standing silent, a little in the background, Caine forward and said respeetfrilly, "You mustn't stay much longer, miss, you mustn't indeed, or we shall lose that train and be late for dinner, and then your pa will find out where you have been." "What shalrl do" cried the girl in" a tot& of anguish. "She litiows all 'about it, and she won't tell me ! If is really cruel of you I ,she Said to Anne. "Tell me exactly what it is you want to know,'.' she answered, compaasionating the girl's distreas,and yet hardening her heart against conceding anything /which would endanger tier seoret, "I will gladly help you, if I cap." "I want to know whether that diamond was really, lost, or whether he has given it away, or what has become of it. He looked so awfully angry., when I asked him why he never wore the sleeve-links now. Has some woman—some dreadful woman, got them?" said the,, girl under her breath, "that is what I want to find out. And I gave them to him myself on his last birthday," she added, with almost a sob. It was evident now that she—an innocent sufferer —was overshadowed by this dark crime, as well as Anne herself. "Poor girl" she thought, "I am trying to make her unconsciously betray some one she loves, but I .cannot help it. At whatever cost, to any one else, Martin must be saved." . "He is your husband perhaps 1" asked Anne. "No, oh no—not yet." " But going to be ?" "I don't know—not if he is false to me. as I beg,in to think he is." Mid again there was poignant grief in the girrs voice. "You'ought to be saved from marrying him, that is plain enough. I believe he has been false to. you, and- if you *Mild only tell' me his' name and where' he lives, I believe I.cmild prove it." At that momenta distant whistle sounded. The maid cried out in terror, " Miss, you must come, you must—you'll lose the train, and then what will be- come of us?" „ She seized the girl by the arm and absolutely ford-her to run 'towards the bridge. Anne was desperate; at the very instant that she thought victory was in her grasp it was snatched from her. She rushed after the two women. "You'll give nie your name—you'll write to me?" she cried, "My name is—no, I can't tell you now. I'll write, perhaps," the girl gasped mit as she ran. Anne pursued her over the bridge, and up the' hill towards the railway station. It so happened that three half-tipsy men were coming down the footpath arm in arm, blocking up the svay. The girl and her maid darted into . the road .to avoid them Anne tried tOdo the same, but somehow she slipped on the kerb-stohe and fell right down upon the road. She' was not hurt, and the men passed on without noticing her; but in rising again she entangled her foot in hei gown, and the minute's' delay was fatal. As she rushed into the station the train was jot moving out. ' Anne" looked up and down the platform, in- credulous that the two women could have escaped her. But they were nowhere to he seen. Then she east dew* on the wooden bench, put up her hands to • her forehead, and felt that a very little more Would deprive her of her senses. She was aroused by Richards coming up to her 'with a look of concern. "Be you hurted any way, miss? I was skeered when I saw you get that nasty tumble, but I couldn't kite!' you up More, there was such a lot of people got in my way a-coming out of the station." "No, I am not hurt," replied Anne a little wildly. "Only--I feet like to die. • There, never mind, Richards, I shall be better presently. I. have only one more thing to de, and then—rn go home." The one thing was to question the railway officials. Had they noticed a lady, quite young, a little deformed, dressed in a brown ulster end felt hat! one had a maid with nor, a very respectatne looking, middle-aged woman. Did anybody happen to know to what station they were going?.' "Back to Plymouth, I reckon," said the ticket collector. They came up by .the 5.41. . .1 know they gave me two halves of •return ticicets frehn Plymouth to Tavistock. I happened to notice the young lady you speak of, she was a bit humpbacked, poor soul, as you were saying. But I don't know as I ever saw her before, and who she is, Icouldn't tell you, if there was to be a hundred liound reward offered." So that was all; and Anne returned home, weary,' and sick at heart; yet knowing amid her bitter dis- appointment that she had advanced somestenefurther

DS Parker i without hard labour. has denied that he received stneepayment fordeliver- ' ing the eulogy on W ard Beecher. The statement to the conteetry is categorically made in a letter dated the 18th otNovember, which Miejor Pond, his agent, wrote ts rkhe secretary of the Beecher Memorial Committee. Major Pond therein says ".I paid all the bills pertaining to that Address, and I paid Dr. Parker for his services." .This conflict of statement probably seises out of the diverse ways of regarding a simple act. WI.. Parker acknowledges that he re- ceived a cheque for 700 dollars in connection with the eulogy. But he says it was an account of his expenses, and ,dfd not meet them by a hundred dollars. Whateeer the payment was meant for, the fact is indisputed that Dr. Parker presented the cheque as a contribution to the Reecho! Memorial, for which he aeoeived the warm thanks of the :eommittee. s' English Newspapers "have found a worthy his- torian in Mr, Fox :Bourne, whose work under this title Misers. Chatte and Windus have just issued in two handsome 'volumes. Beginning with the birth of the newspaper,. Mr. Bourne comes down to the pre- sent day, which makes his work a delicate one. He haeehowever, discharged it with great tact, skewing a knowledge of the Inside history of the famous newspapers of to-day, which is not less remarkable for its accuracy than for its extent. I happen to have some personal knowledge of one or two of the journals Mr. Bourne deals with, and can testify to the soundness of his inforination. It is a singularly interesting story, from the first page to the last. Mr. Kinglake is the object of many congratulations on the conclusion of his herculean labours. I am not quite certain whether there is not some modicum of self-gratulation In the compliments now lavished upon him. It was all very well for Homer to write his account of the siege of Trey at such length and with such detail. People had more leisure in thc.se days. For us to-day Mr. Kinglake's conception of dealing with an episode of history is a little embarrassing. To read the forty volumes of his "Invasion of the Crimea," from the first page to the last, is a task almost as formidable as the storming of the !Wan. -It is a great work, full of patches of brilliant writing, a model of patieoce, industry, and application. But for perfect success it is too long, out of all proportion BM to the imeleeentous event it describes.. I :

' During a violent "westerly gale in the Tine on Stflur.: . . day a boat employed in carrying ships' stores, II - towing behind a steam lighter, was upset. The man In charge of it was thrown into the water and drowned.i. The barque Eljemlos, bound 'from Belfast, in bittisit, went ashore on Rhoscoiwyn Point, near Holyhead, on Sunday, and. became 'a total loss. The crew-wits rescued by the coastguard life-saving apparatus. During a severe gale on Seturday a small vessel, the Royal Standard, of Bridgwater, was wrecked rota.. Port Ballintrae Strand, near Bushtnills, connty Antrim. rine captain and one of the crew were saved, but two men were divivned.. The ,yessel, which was Jades with cement, became siotai wreck.. . Early 'on sSt.turilay 'morning there was a. fresh gale blowing at the mouth of the Mersey from N.N.W. The schooner Alice Figier, a vessel of about 100 tons,, and owned by Mr. J<ilin 'Fisher. of Beirrow, went ashore on what is known as Taylor's Bank, off Formby. A serious steamship- oollision took place on Saturday morning on the Clyde, Oft the Pladda Light, between the Allan Line steamer Manitoban, from Glasgow for Philadelphia, and the Donaldson Line steamer Alcides. from Boston for Glasgow. The morning was dark and stormy, and the Manitoban was proceeding down the river, sounding her whistles. The lights of the incoming steamer were suddenly seen, and a violent cq.tlision fol.. lowed, the Manitolain -striking the Alcides with ouch force that the latter-wits cut down to the watet's edge, while the former had her bows stove in. Both vessels were towed to the Tail of the Bank. and the-Alcides started for Glasgow, but she grounded above Greenock. •

WESLEYAN QUARTERLY MEETING.-- 7W aletßinti4 alnetrU• -Thequarterly meeting of the Wesleyan Methodists I,cet; the Warringt.b. Cireuitc as held jon. play. at Bold-skreet Chapel *Lal'ge'Vestry The 'was. a large attendance at tea; and afterwards a cordial vote of thanks was accorded to Mrs. T. S. Smith and Mrs. W. Sileock for the ability with which they had •discharged their duties during the year. At the Meeting the Rev. G. E Young presided, and .amongst those present were Rev. W. Brookes, Rev. E. H. Jackson; and. Messrs. Lawton, W. Barlow, Richardson, Henshall, John Bennett, Shaw Green, .Summersgill..„Braithwaitet Butler, Taylor, R. Garnett, Dale, Brough. BindersOn, W. Silcock, florttin, Light, F. Wright, and Dr. Gomall. A hymn was sung, and Rev. W. Brookes engaged in prayer.— The finan— ciar statement was read and confirmed. The , deficiency on circuit account was upwards of £7O. This was mainly attributable to the fact that -conaider- able expense had been incurred in changing one of the ministers' houses. In order to meet this it was resolved, on the proposition of the eirciiit steward, and seconded by Mr. W. Barlow, that this deficiency be placed With and form part of a town or cirmiitscheme, with a view to assist the trustees of some of the chapels to liquidate certain debts that have been or are likely to be incurred, that may be decided upon at a meeting of the trustees Bold-st., Bewseproad, and Silver-4., to be hpl in January; and that in the event of this proposed sebefne not being floated, then a special effort be made to clear off this deficiency. The Chairman reported the number of meinbers to be 920. A cordial • and unanimous vote of thanks was given to Dr. Starkey Smith and Mr. W. Sileock for their services as circuit stewards. Dr. Starkey Smith having expressed a wish to retire from office, Mr. W. Sikock was iniani- mouslv re-appointed as senior circuit steward. On the nomination of the Chairman, Mr. R. G. Hensball was unanimously chosen to represent the interests of Metho- dism inthe circnit as Mr. Silcock's colleague. Thatest thanks of the meeting were accorded to Mr. Robt. Cook for his very efficient services as chapel secretary. The circuit trustees' meetingwill Jae held on the same day as the March quarterly meeting. Mr. W. Y. Lawton was thanked for his services as treasurer of the home hire fund, and re-appointed. Mr. R. Garnett proposed with unusual pleasure, aridit was seconded very cordially by Mr. John Bennett, and it was supported by Mr. Shaw Green, that the hearty thanks of the 'meeting be given to the local preachers for their efficient leriices in the cir- cuit. The Chairman having wished those present a merry Christmas and a very happy new year, the Doxo- logy was supg, the Benediction pronounced, and' a very pleasant meeting terminated.

div.head: lIR. T. MORRIS'S GERMAN CLASS.
div.p: lIR. T. MORRIS'S GERMAN CLASS.

In connection with the class of students some time ago formed under the auspices of Mr. T. Morris to study the German 'language, ,an entertainment vies given on Wednesday evening at Bank House, Warrington. The Mayor (Alderman Sutton) pre- sided, and there was a full attendance, among those. present being the Mayoress; the Misses Garland. Alderman Pickmere, Rev. S. and Mrs. Wilkinson, Dr. Peacock, ite. . The Mayor mentioned that letters of apolegy for non- , attendance had been received from Mr. Beamont, Mr. It. Davies, Mr. E. J. Wileoeks, Sir Gilbert Greenall, and Alderman Crosfield. They, all knew, he continued, that they had come there that night to witness and listen to a play in the German language. That was gather a novelty in Warrington, and he did not know that he had I ever heard any play performed in any language but their I own. It was, therefore, at all events so far as he was concerned, a novelty. That class of students of German had now been studying about three-quarters of a-year, and he understood that they had made very considerable progress. He was sure that was very gratifying to Mr. Morris, who had taken such an interest in the young men of Warringtori as to encourage them in the way he had ta learn the Prep...Tian language, and he believed that it was entirely due to Mr. Morris that that -class was formedond,that he had made himself responsible forl , a Considerable portion of the expense in connection with it. (Applause.) Mr. Morris had always taken a deep ' interest in young men, and especially at the time when they were just leaving school, and it had annoydd him very much to know that they in England were not hold- ' ing their own with .other countries in the nrat,ter of languages for while, as a rule, Germans could speak two or three languages, there were very few Englishmen who could speak more than their own native tongue. The Mayor also referred to the fact that there were numerous' situations in English mercantile houses, and other estab- lishments, held by Germans, but which would haye been held by Englishmen had the latter had a better know- I ledge of foreign languages. (Hear, hear.) ' An overture was then admirably played on the piano by Mddle. Blanchet and Miss Harrison, and ' this was followed by a recitation "William Tell's I address to his native hills and crags" by. Mr. A. Perris, in his usual effective style. The feature of the evening was, however, the scene from Schiller's." Wilhelm Tell.", in which the students of the first class took part. Although not in costume, the performers entered with zest into the spirit of the play, and their acting through- out did them great credit. Gessler, the tyrant, could not have had a better impersonator than Mr. Hayes, while Mr. Bouebier was equally happy La his character qf "Wilhelm Tell." In the first part of the scene—the Arrest of Tell—Messrs. Brookes and R. Tholeeley, as akuthold and Frie,szhardt came to the front, and their spirited acting in the altercation with the friends of Tell was much appreciated. The other characters were sustained as follows : Rudenz, Mr. L. Chandler; Walter Tell, Mr. Fieldhouee ; Sigrist, Mr. Howard; Walter Furst, Mr. C. George; Ros.selmann (a priest), Mr. Calvert; Stauffacher, Mr. Pilkington; Melchthal, Mr. Gandy. Iriluring the interval the Mayor, in a few neatly ex- pressed words, presented Mddle. Blanchet, in the name of her pupils in both classes, with a handsome volume, "The Dore Gallery," and some handkerchiefs from Mrs Morris. At the request of Mddle., Mr. Thomas Morris thanked the students for their generous gift, and con- gratulated teacher and pupils on the efficiency displayed by the latter in the play they had just witnessed. In the severe competition of to-day, he said, it behoved young men to seize every opportunity they could 6 improve themselves in order to hold their own with foreigners. In most of the offices in London, Liverpool, Manchester, and other large towns, the chief places were filled by Germans who could speak, beside their own language, English and French, and these classes had been got up to enable the youn_g men of Warrington to compete suc- cessfully with thee aliens, and with their own weapons to drive them out of the country. (Applause.) The Rev. R. Wilkinson said that it was the fashion now-a-days to depreciate English education, but he thought that if it was not the best, it was at least manly, and though there was a tendency to overdo athletics, yet we might go to the other extreme and fare worse. (hear, hear.) Alderman Pick:mere in a few words compared the education/of his day with that of to-day, and hoped that the students would fully help out Mr Morris in his scheme for their improvement by keeping manfully to their work. (Hear, hear.) Mr. J. Roberts, well known at entertainments of this kind as a violinist of great ability, then treated the audience with selections from " Maritana," which were exceedingly well received. This was followed by a scene from Moliere's " L'Avare," Mr. Bouchier again ably representing Harpagon, the suspicious miser; Mr. Lincoln Chandler effectually supporting the part of La Fleche. A song from Mr. W. E. Atkin' and a violin duet "Viennese Dense," in which Mr. J. Roberts again took part, assisted by Mr. Atkin came next, and a pianoforte trio by Mddle. Blanchet and the Misses Geddes completed the programme for the evening. A vote of thanks to the Mayor for presiding was carried, and a pleasant evening terminated with a vote of thanks to Mr. Thomas Morris, the Rev. S. Wilkinson in propos- ing it saying that great praise was due to Mr. Morris for having originated, and with large-souled liberality borne the expenses of these German classes, and he could not sitdown without mentioning also the ready kindness of the Misses Garland in lending them the room.

In September there were- 275 fresh cases, in October 498,. November CO4, December (up to the 19th inst.,:) 535. The epidemic began in March with three caies. Donors of prizes not included in this list are re- quested to communicate with the secretary of the Christmas Prize Committee, Drill Hall. The following comprise the Prize Committee :---Sergt.- Major Fennelly, Sergeant-Instructor Birch, Quarter- master-Sergiant Heaton, Paymaster-Sergeant Wei- mough, Sergeant Bugler Plinston, Pioneer-Sergeant War- burton, Sergeant-master-cook Cliffe Hospital-Sergeant Mycock, Colour-Sergeant Plinston, CA;lour-Skrgeant Bate, Colour-Sergeant Hewitt, Sergeant Tunics, Sergeant Wood, Sergeant Jolley, Sergeant Ward, Sergeant Painter, Sergeant Lee, Sergeant Ilenmon, Sergeant Stirrup, Ser- geant Ice, Sergeant Johnson, Sergeant Bebbington, Ser- geant Daniels, Sergeant Denham, and Sergeant Kidd, O.R.C. Secretary'. After the distribution a cordial vote of thanks was awarded the donors of the prizes on the motion of Col. Bolton, seconded by Capt. Ridgway. Capt. Buckton also moved a vote of thanks to the Christmas Prize Com- mittetcand this was also warmly accorded. In respond- ing Sergt. Watmough proposed a vote of thanks to Col. Bolton and officers of the corps for their attendance that night. This brought the proceedings to a close. The prizes won in F Company competition were also distributed. In this competition there is a cup presented by Captain Gooch, with £l, and made up into Z 4 by sergeants of company for the purpose of encouraging shooting. Owing to alteration of the range some diffi- culty has arisen in completing this competition, and the conditions have had to be slightly altered this year in order to enable class firing to be completed with as' little delay as possible, so that instead of firing seven rounds at 200 and 300 yards in the first stage as before, the three highest scores in each squad, when class firing, have been taken to compete in the final stage, viz., seven rounds 300 and 400 yards—which was to have been completediast Saturday, but unavoidably postponed owing to rain, &c. The following are winners of prizes in first competion :-Ist Squad Private H. Hewitt, 53 points, lOs; Private W. STRALING LORD Dawn's Pnintsmrrs.—At the Prescot Petty Sedsions on Tuesday, before Messrs. F. W. Earle and W. Gibson, James Murray, a rough-looking man, described as a labourer at Presc.ot, was charged with stealing a pheasant valued at 2s k, the property of Lord Derby. P.C. Jackson stated that at half-past four on the afternoon of the 15th inst., he saw the prisoner going through Knowsley Park. He. noticed something bulky under hie coat and searched him, whereupon he found-the pheasant produced. It was dead, but the body was quite warm. The prisoner said he had found it near Knowsley old farm and was taking it home.— John Barnes; head gamekeeper for Lord Derby, deposed that a shooting'party was in the Park on the day in ' question. He saw the prisoner in the Park and ordered him away. The pheasant was worth 2s 6d.—The priso- ner pleaded guilty, and Superintendent Barker said he was a very bad character, He had been 15 tlm; pre- viously convicted. He was committed feria month with hard labour. CONCERT AT. GOLBORWS. A large and appreciative audience assembled in the Congregational Schools, Gol- borne, on Friday evening, when under the auspices of the Ebenezer Lodge of Good 'Temp:ars an enjoyable con- cert and entertainment was given. The chair was oc- ccuiedby Mr. Gear Clark, of Earlestown, who com- menced the proceedings with an appropriate addEgii: Mr. James Prescott, of Edge Green, gave a planoftirte soio after which Miss Sutton (Ashton) sang "The 'blind orphan girl." The Rev. J. Roberts-Evans, of Wigan, next gave an impressive rendering of "The collier's elving child," for which he was warmly ap- plauded. During the evening he also gave "The burial of Moses," " The vision of Belshazzar," "The Spanish champion," "Beautiful Snow," "Charge of the Light Brigade," "The old armchair," and "Casablanca." He was deservedly appreciated, and met with a hearty commendation. Mr. It. Owen (Earlestown) sang "The yachtsrnan" ; Miss Whittle (Haydock) sang" Eternity;', Miss Rees and Mr. R. H. Jones (Newton) gave the duet "Love and pride " ; Mr. J. Garsie (St. Helens) sang "My mother-in-lan • Miss Owen (Earlestown) sang "Tit for tat " ; Mr. Jolla Gorse (St. Helens) sang " Doc- tor Gregory " ; Mr. and Miss Owen (Earlestown) gave the duet "The soldier's farewell" ; Miss fleets sang " Olivia " ; Miss Rees and Mr. It. HI Jones sang the duet "Very suspicious " ; Messrs. Gorse , (St. Helens).and T. Martindale (Earlestown) gave "The upper ten and the lower five"; Mr. R. Owen sang "The young brigade 't Miss Whittle "The beautiful city " ; Miss Owen Allan , water " ; and Miss Sutton, "A flower from father's grave." An enjoyable entertainment then closed with the "National Anthem."
