div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, DECEMBER 24,1887.

Loan SALISBURY'S speech at Derby on Monday was looked forward to with more than ordinary interest, from the fact that it was believed he would have something definite to say as to the Fair Trade doctrine adopted .by the Conservative 'Conference which met at Oxford the other day. His lordship spoke out pretty plainly on the sub- ject, but his plainness must have been painful to -the Fair Traders who were sitting beside him. As in duty bound—for he was amongst his own sup- porters—he tried to "let them down easy;" but we rather think that ,the impression on them would be that they were let down with a rattle -and a rush. Perhaps, as his manner is sometimes, he was cruel only to be kin J.. They should remem- ber that he has the Liberal Unionists to please; and that if he were to turn his back upon Free Trade, as he has turned his back upon so many of his opinions, they would turn their back; upon him, and he would go to the wall. He began by saying that he was not going to express any opinion on the subject (though there could be no mistake as to his opinion in the end), and the reason that he gave for his reticence was anything but complimentary to those who have for so many I months been trying to make it out that Fair Trade is as clear as noon day, and as good as gold. He said:—

I abstain from expressing any opinion about it for a reason which may seem to you inadequate and inapplicable, for the reason that I do not know ex; actly what it means. I have the greatest respect for many of those by whom the word is used; I have great sympathy for the un- pubted and real and most cruel sufferings out of which the desire for some such remedy has sprung; but I wait with respectful attention until the demands of those who ask far Fair Trade are embodied in the only form in -which my unimaginative intelligence ii capablq of comprehending—(laughter)—them, namely, as clauses of a bill presented to Parliament. I have • listened to and read carefully all that has been said about Pair Trade, and I hare observed this, that there are many point): on which they are agreed and many points on which they are precise ; but upon thosn points, on which they are precise they are not agreed, and upon those points on which they are agreed they are not precise. (Laughter and cheers.) . This is another and only a little more polite way 'of saying, with Mr. JOHN BRIGHT, that the Fair Traders are a silly set of people who do not know • what they are about. But Lord SALISBURY went further; he made it clearly understood that the Government did not regard themselves as in any respect bound to the resolution which Mr. HOWARD VINCENT • carried at the . Conservative Conference.

I must, he said, protest most energetically be- cause my honourable friend on this platform has passed a motion in favour, of Fair Trade, I must protest most energetically 'against the impression that it is to follow that Her Majesty's Government are pledged to the doctrines of Protection. We have always and on all opeasions frankly 'expressed our opinion that the protection of corn, that the advo- cacy of such a doctrine, is very unwise, and that the prospect of such a measure being carried into effect, even if it were expedient, which I don't think it is, is absolutely out of the bounds of politi- cal possibility. (Cheers.) - • - -

Where do the Fair Traders stand after this declaration? If there is one thing more patent than another when the question of Fair Trade or Protection is considered, it is that, if any. thing is to be done at all, it must be done for the suffering agriculturist. The National Fair Trade League admit this. At the recent meet- ing at Warrington they went the whole hog of a duty on corn; but Lord SALISBURY says "the protection of corn" is." absolutely out of the bounds of political possibility." The Fair Traders are met point-blank with an unequivocal.denial ;• and it is interesting to see what they will do. They have preached about Fair Trade as though the very life of the nation depended upon its adoption. They have pushed their advocacy until their creed has been adopted by a representative body of conservatives; and now when they might have thought themselves as most important, they are thrown overboard as so much useless I=l3er. If they are sincere, if they are as much in earnest as they pretend to be, they will immediately Con- demn the SALISEURY Administration just as freely as they denounced the GLADSTONE Government. 'They were never tired, when Mr. GLansrorra was, in office, of urging that he stood in the way of good. trade by rejecting Fair Trade. But now we have Lord SALISBURY taking up the very same position, and if the movement ;s not, as we suspect it is, being made use of to catch votes amongst the un- thinking, we shall see the Fair Traders cutting themselves aloof from party, and pushing their doctrines irrespective of either side. No doubt it will be urged that Lord SALISEURY says he refrains from expressing an opinion; but we have shown that as to the cardinal point—a duty on corn—he ..,sists that such a thing is impossible. And if that be the case, what is there left for the Fair Traders to trade on? Will they have tbe hardi- hood to ask the wer-nigh ruined farmer to pay more for every implement he uses in order that manufacturers may obtain, for a time, a larger in- terest on • their capital? And if they do show themselves so case-hardened, will they be likely to get the farmer's vote? The Fair Traders are cor- nered; they have fought their way to the front: they have asked for "a moderate duty on corn :" and Lord SALISBURY, while professing to withhold his opinion, says, with startling emphasis, that they cannot have that. They will perhaps see after a 'while that his lordship is laughing at them —that he looks upon their formless theory as "a tale told by an idiot, full of found and fury, signi- fiing nothing."

One of the most interesting volumes in the Eng- lish Men of Letters series, published by Messrs. MACMILLAN & Co., is that on EDMUND BURKE, 'by Mr. JOHN MORLEY. Bunxn was a Whig who developed, so the Tories claim, into one of the greatest Tories of the day. There can he no question that he was essentially conservative, using the word in its best sense, and that he was as .honest as he was fervent in denouncing the authors of the French Revolution. He had a strong love of order, and of orderly modes of redressing grievances; but he recognised above all things that there was such a thing as justice, and that it was the duty of governors to deal justly by the people they governed. His name has fre- quently of late figured in speeches and letters on the Irish question; but, after reading his life by Mr. JOHN MORIEY, we are at a loss to see what either the Tories or the Liberal Unionists have to gain by appealing to the teachings of the great Irishman. He took the side of JOHN WILKES when Parliament refused to accept him as a mem- ber—just as he would have sided with CHARLES BRADLAUGH, had he been living when' the Tories Mused to allow him to take his seat in the House of Commons. He sagely remarked as to the' agitation in 'Mums' days that "the people are commonly right whenever they have a feeling, though they sometimes mistake the physician?' Again, at the beginning of the struggle which ended in the loss of our American colonies, he said : "I am not one of those who think the people are never wrong. They have been so frequently and outra- geously, both .in other countries,and in this. But I do say in all disputes between them and their rulers the presumption is at least upon a par in favour of the people." Apply this to the Irish question and what does it suggest? Lord SALIS- BURY and Lord BARTINGTON would have LIS believe that the Irish have no serious cause of complaint; but, seeing that the dispute with Government has lasted through the whole of the present cen- tury, we would ask—ls it not time to consider whether they may not be in the right and their rulers in the wrong ? , It is suggested that' the Irish resist the law out of sheer, malevolence; but 13unxn says, speaking in general terms—" The people have no interest in disorder. When they go wrong, it is their error and not their crime." What have the Coercionist admirers of BURKE to say to this? Perhaps, as the only loophole of es- cape, they will contend that the Irish as a people are the one exception which proves the rule; but those who have seen how brutally they have been misgOverned and coerced Voow too well that they have been provoked to disorder in a thousand ways. Further, "the revolutions that come to pass in great states are not the result of chance, or of popular caprice. As for the populace, it is never from a passion for attack that it rebels, but from impatience of suffering." This was said, not in regard to Ireland, but how true'it is of Ireland! The masses in every country are, for the most part, patient drudges ; and, if they are fairly fed and fairly housed they will submit to see those who are set in authority over them riot in luxury. It is when, as in Ireland, the bit of land that they have redeemed from the barren hill- side is torn from them, and the cabin they have built levelled to the ground because they fail to 'pay an impossible rent, that they rebel against tyranny and wrong. And they have a right to rebel; their discontent is divine; it is the herald of a better state of things. As 13unxz finely puts it in his speech on the war with the colonists:—" The .question with me is not whether you have a right to render your people miserable, but whether it is not your interest to make them happy. It is not what a lawyer tells me I may do, but what humanity, reason, and justice tell me I ought to do. I am not determining a point of law; lam restoring tranquility, and the general character and situa- tion of a people must determine what sort of go- vernment is fitted for them." Whig or Tory, these are the words of a wise and humane statesman, and we would that the Whigs and Tories of to-day would ever bear them in mind when they consider what should be done with Ireland. If they revere BURKE, let them act in the spirit of his teaching. They will then deal justly with the people of Ire- land by granting Home Rule.

Mr. JOHN WHITE seems to have taken it to heart that Mr. JOHN CROSFIELD should have stated that "the object of the Fair Trade cry was to put money into landowners' pockets, and to raise the screw of the agent." He acknowledges that he is a landlords' agent, but wishes it to be understood that he is paid not by commission, but by a fixed salary which is not affected by the rise or fall of rents. Happy agent! who is always sure of his pound of flesh. But granting this, it is still pertinent to ask Mr. WHITE whether, seeing that his salary is a first charge on the estate, it is, not expected of him that he will do the very best he can for his principal; and whether, if he believed Fair Trade would increase rent, he would not think it his duty to advocate Fair Trade? The point, after all, apart from Mr. CROSFIELD'S jocular way of putting it, is really whether a landlords' agent can be regarded as wholly disinterested in supporting a ' movement which obviously aims at putting money. into • landlords' pockets. It was very wrong, of course, for the Liberal candidate for Warrington to deal with the matter in a jocular way; for Mr: WHITE is nothing if he is not serious. He can, to be sure, quote Shakespeare, and accur an opponent (without ground, so far as we can observe) of posing as Sir Oracle. But then he Usually takes a jaundiced view of things, for has not

Melancholy marked him for her own? If he could but have a laugh with Mr. CROSFIELD, he would not have had other people laughing at him. But, as his favourite author has it— Seldom he SmiliZ and smiles in such a sort An if he mocked himself and scorned his spirit , That could be moved to smile at anything. It seems itis another grievance with Mr. WHITE that Mr. CROSFIELD'S sentences are not "as rounded as those of DEMOSTHENES." But if they had been, is it not just possible, after that touch- ing reference to "the screw of the agent," tha:; 'Mr. WHITE would have " rounded " on him all the same P It is;at any rate, to he said for Mr. CROS- FIELD that he has not at any time suggested that he takes DEMOSTHENES for his model ; so that if he falls short in this respect it cannot be said to be a failure. The fact is, he does not ape any'- body ; he is one of those who believe that An honest tale speeds besi: being plair'y told. But what shall we say of Mr. WHITE, when like dainty ARIEL, he in effect exclaims:— • Bid me discourse! I will enchant thine ear!

He does discourse—he was. discourein; on Monday night—but whore, oh where, is the enchantment P He speaks, it is true, after the manner of DEMOS- nimins—a long way after-.--3ome of his critics may be inclined to. say; but it should be remem- bered that Damosxnasras wal not confined to one style. ,There is early,DP.ilosruzwEs as well as early English; and it is. just possible that Mr. WHITE fitT1111(14118A a successful imitation of the effect which prevailed when the great Athenaaan orator

practised on the sea shore with pebbles in his. mouth. Well, well, taste is everything, even in. oratory, and, if Mr. WHITE will be Demostiienic, so be it,- always providing that, being left to do as he likes, he will leave others to please themielves —to follow the model they prefer, or, if they think fit, to be without Model, and thus maybe To snech a grace beyond the reach of art.

"Toren ANDI4O." Reader, pray thee, accept— The warm wish that these winter eves inspire— "A merry Christmas and a glad New Year." This is a stock sentiment, but there is no reason why it should not be sincere. Sunshine is a stock thing, but it never ceases to be pleasant; and good wishes are the sunshine of the heart. But good wishes may be more than sunshine; they become a plent;ful harvest when they resolve themselves into deeds. And who is there that cannot do something ? "Christmas is here, the day of good cheer" ; but let your good cheer go beyond eating and drinking.

There is the postman for instance; he of the G.P.O.— general poor object..--" an you love him do not treat him to "a good stiff glass." It is very bad treatment indeed; in the end it is any- thing but good, and a very stiff price has been paid for it when the postman loses his post for neglect (32 duty. The postman is type of a class; so if you have anything to give, reader, let it be a cue of "soft words and hard cash." •

It was rumoured that Lord Randolph Churchill was going to Seville to eat oranges; but it trans- pires that he has goue to Russia to see what the bear is like. But he may get more than he bar- gains for; he may catch the bear—and a cold.

Lord Salisbury did ill to those who do well when he sneered, oil Monday, at the .efforts of teeth- tailors. Where has he been, not to know that there are temperance clubs as well as political clubs? But perhaps he does know, and has discovered that when men cease dtioking and take to thinking they, as a rule, become Ralical. Having bettered them- selves, they cane see their way to bettering the con- dition oft ieir kind.

Prize fighting is having a sort of revival. On lioilday, Smith, an Englishman, and Kilrain, an American, fought for the championship on the Seine, between Paris and Rouen. There was quite a rush out of London of " genteel " blackguards, in order to be present at the fight. The brutal contest ended in a draw, so that he betting came to nothing. It is one satisfactory feature of the fight that it did not take place on English ground.

The report of the Hon. S. L. Stanley on the bankrupt Cardiff Savings Bank does not mince matters. It shows that the managers and other officials have been shamefully negligent. Some of them are rich men whose names were paraded to give 'confidence to investors. As they have lea undone that which they ought to hay.e done, it will serve them rlght if they are called upon, as they may be, to Make good the deficit.

The slippery state of the roads, yesterday, com- bined with the dense fog rendered it difficult alike for horses and men to keep on their feet. The attitudes struck by pedestr!ans on thiai high roads were wonderful in their variety' the stained-glass attitude was "not in it." There will, of course be a change in the weather for Christmas. The clerk of that department does not fura'sh the same supply for two days to- gethez.

A German paper says that Hoffman, the boy pianist, objected recently to pay a vidit to the house of an English gentleman. On being asked why he refused, he said: "There are too many English ladies there. They cut locks off my hair, I must writs all day long in their albums, and they kiss me from morning to night, and I don't care for it." Poor fellow He will perhaps care for it when he is ten years older. And then he won't got it, eh? Such is life.

We were puzzled the other day to know why, on certain estates, cheap wire fences were being taken down and replaced by expensive wood fences. But the murder is out; it is because wire fences do not suit fox-hunters, and what is agriculture to hunt: ing ? As Lord John Manners might say, in a new edition:— Let laws and learning, arts and commerce die; .I.Aa everything go fearfully awry; Let farmers struggle with misfortune dire, But spare, oh spare, the hunting country squire:

It seems that the Rev. T. Nattrass, who died suddenly on Sunday, whilst conducting service ii Bowdon Wesleyan Chapel, had been hurrying. somewhat to be in time for the service. At the inquest on Tuesday, Dr. Golland said such a death as his was caused in nine times out of ten by hurry.. The lesson is a painful one.; people who. are known to have weak hearts should contrive, whenever tkey possibly can, to take time by the forelock, and husband their strength. The creak- ing gate may hang long if not suddenly strained.

As the result of the International Congress on Sugar Bounties, which has been sitting at the Foreign Office, it is likely that there will be an end of the bouaty system; and some of the supporters of the Government are pluming themselves not a little on the achievement. But there is not much to be proud of. We may be quite sure that the bounty givers would have held by the system if it paid them to do so. They ara getting tired of this form of Protection at any rate; and if they give it up, we in this country may have to pay more for our sugar—that is all.

The.4;!eath of the Rev. A. H. Mackonochie from exposure among the Scotch hills will be sad a loss to that section of the Church party for whom he made so stout a fight. He went out with two dogs with him, and was lost in the storm on Thursday night week. He was found lying dead in the snow at an early hour on Saturday morning, the two dogs sitting beside the body. What a picture of faithfulness! Who is there that does not sympathise with the poor Indian who dreams of heaven, and— , thinks admitted to that equal sky His faithful dog shall bear him company ?

The Clerk to the Warrington Board of Guar- dians was right on Wednesday in pointing out that there was a sort of understanding between in- dividuals who lived outside the borough and the Corporation for the use of the fire engine to put out fires: but there :was no arrangement for the use of the Fever Hospital in case of infectious disease. But whose fault is that ? Not the fault of the Corporation, surely ? If the Rural Sanitary Authority think too much is asked for the use of the Warrington Hospital, why do they not set about providing a hospital of their own? At present, with smallpox in their midst, they stand in the position of a man who allows a fire to rage because he is disposed to haggle about the cost of a fire engine.

A Runcorn puhlican has been fined 20s. and costs for keeping his house open during prohibited hours, notwithstanding the pleading of his lawyer that no charge had ever before been brought against him. There is a story told of a weaver who, on being fined by his overlooker for being late, appealed to the master. He did not think he ought to be fined—he had never been late be- fore. "And have you ever been fined before for being late?" "How could I?" was the answer. "There, now," said the master, "you see how fair the arrangement is—you have only. been late on,-3, and you-have only been fined once. What could be,better ?" The weaver went back to his work with a new light on the subject.

WIDNES GYMNASIUM RARRIARS.—The members of the above club indulged in a good spin on Saturday, in spite of the inclemenay of the weather. They left the Millfield Inn at about 3-30, and proceeded over the fields to Apple- ton village, then across a few more fields and along the road to the Ball Inn, Ditton, and then to Hough Green. From Hough Green they made for Cronton, and then turned for horns past the Black Hctse and on through Farnworth. Mier a smart fitiish J. Kelly reached home Ist, Cowley, 2nd, and Etheridge 3rd, Roscoe, McMahon, Franklin. Brocklehurst, &c., finishing indiscriminately. The following have been elected officers of the club : J. Roscoe, captain; P. J. McMahon and G. Etheredge, sub-captains; F. Franklin, hon. sec. and treasurer. FREE PUBLIC LECTURE AT WIDNES.—The second of the series of free public lectures arranged for by the Library Committee was given in Lacev-street schoolroom on Tuesday evening. Mr. FL Wane Deacon, chairman of the committee, presided, and there was a capital attend- ance. Mr. V. C. Driffield repeated his lecture on " Pho- tography," in which he trac3d the development of the art from its inception. The lecture was illustrated with limerght views of photographs taken by Mr. Driffield in the locality, and places further afield; and, in the presence of the audience, Mr. Driffield enlarged an or- dinary carte de visit of the chairman to life size. An enjoyable evening was brought to a close by, the custom- ary votes of thanks. The next lecture will be on the subject of "African Exploration," by Mr. T. Snape ; and at a later date Dr. Hinter treat of "The Philo- sopher's Stone." RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.—The monthly meetirg was held on Wednesday under the presidency of Mr. W. Handley. The chairman introduced the question of providing literature specially interesting to lathes in the reading room. It was stated that ladies were at liberty to partake of the benefits of the reading room, and it was decided, to maka :t more attractive to them, to place on the table the "London Pictorial," "Queen," and "Woman's World." The advisability of allowing retideats just outsid3 the boundaries of the Runcorn Improvement District the privilege of using the Lending Library was ctinsidered. It was thought that persons li*.:ng in Halton and Weston mioht have the pris _lege on the payment of a small annual subscription, and the' librarian (Mr. J. D. Jones) NW instructed to as- certain the practice in other public libraries. The librarian reported that during Noven4ier 1831 books were issued. .

In consideration of the fact that the prisoner had beea remanded in gaol for a week, the Bench sentenced him to seven days hard labour. WIDNES COUNCIL OF EDUCATION. Yesterday week the prizes awarded to the scholars of Simm's Cross School, by the Council of Education, were presented by Mr. J. W. Waring. The value of the prizes are as fol- lows :-Ist, 2s. and a silver gilt modal; 2nd, 2s. and a certificate; and 3rd, 2s. only. To obtain the highest award every possible attendance must be made; whilst those who miss ten attendances are entitled to a second prize. A third prize is earned by only missing 25 atten- dances. Should a scholar be successful—earning a first prize for three years in succession he would receive a silver gilt, a bronze, and a gold gilt medal. The num- ber of prize winners at Similes Cross School are :--Senior boys, let prize, 84 •, 2nd, 50 • 3rd. 38: total, 172. Senior girls, Ist, 30 ; 2nd, 18 ; '3rd, 27; total, 75. WriaNzs GYMNASIIIM.—In connection with this institu- tion, an assaelt-at-arms WAS given in the Baths Assembly Room on Wednesday evening. There Yval only a moderate attendance. Mr. W. E. Oakden explained that this athletic d'splay had been arranged to arouse any latent interest there might be felt by the toss dspeople in the gymnasium. _Last year there were 90 members, but this year there had been a falling off in the membership, and the subscriptions were not sufficient to meet all the expenses. The committee, however, had good reason to believe that if there was sufficient interest taken in the ginmasium by the town the manufacturers would be willing. to lend their aid. He (Mr. Oakden) thought it .woeld be a pity if so excellent and so much needed in- stitution had to be closed, and the committee had decided !to carzy it on for a few weeks longer, and if anybody would like to join they had better send in their names at I once. Mrs. McMahon stated that a few days ago the defendant came home at noon, and because he could not have what he wished for dinner he cursed and swore, and best her in a most shameful manner. He knocked her to the ground with his fist, and struck her on the head so often that she did not know what she was doing. He had been out of work for twelve months, and had never given her a halfpenny during that period. On the night of the day in question he threatened to take her life, and she was obliged to seek the protection of the police from his violenc3. Che was afraid he would carry out his threat.—lnspector Keighley said he went to the house and spoke to the defendant about his conduct, but he did nothing but sneer and laugh at him.—The defen- dant did not appear, and the Bench issued a: warrant for his apprehension. The xes were there from ten o'clock in the morning until wards evening, and the foot passengers were in- converdenced.—P.C. He was engaged at the back of the shop and could not remove the goods. He had ordered the goods at that time so as not to be encumbered i during Christmas week. He thought he was just:fled in leaving the goods until he could get them removed.—The Bench said there was no doubt the footpath Was obstruc- ted, and imposed a fine of 2s 6d, and cos-:s 8s 6d. STARCED WITH A TABLE KNIFE AT RUNCORN.—At the ' Runcorn Polies CourtAn Tuezday, before Mr. John Brun- drit, a stone breaker named Thomas King was charged with has in feloniously wounded Martin Gilligan with intention to do him grievous bodily harm.—lt appeared that the men were lodging at the lodging house of Mrs. Gibson in MerseY-street, and on Monday evening, whilst having tea, a disagreement arose between them, Gilli- gan called the pesoner a liar, and the prisoner, who is lame, threatened that if he again made use of the expres- s:on he would knock him down. The objectionable ep'thet was again made use of by Gilligan, and the pri- soner seizing an ugly looking table knife stabbed Gilli- gan in the cheek, inflicting a serious wound. The prisoner aimed another blow at Gilligan, who warded off the knife with his hand, and had his knuckles lacerated in so doing. The injured man was taken to the surgerf of Dr. McDougall, who dressed his wounds. Superinten- dent Hollingsworth afterwards went to the lodging-house and arrested the nrisoner. Pointing:to a knife that was on the table, the Superintendent said—" Is this the knife it has been done with ? " The prisorer answered "Yes." Superintendent Hollingsworth informed his worship that Gilligan would not be able to appear for at east a week, and the prisoner was remanded for that period. SAVINGS' BANKS IN LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE. 1 —From a Parliamentary return just issued, it ap- roars - that out of .C 35,937,796 to the credit of depositors in National security savings' banks at the end of last year, £7,491,711 were in Lancashire. Of this 82,625 depositors in the Liverpool Savings' Bank had £2,290.192 to their credit. and the 74.037 depositors in Manchester .C 2,109,310. Among the others of twenty-one banks in the county, Preston with 21,272 depositors and £750,197' was third on the list; followed by Blackburn with 12.007 deptisi-. tors and £436,639, and then Bolton with 6.825 and £302,563, and Warrington with 9.584 and £293,439. The depositors in the twelve banks in Cheshire were credited with .£1,244,111, of which the 1.076 deposi- tors in the Birkenhead bank held £22,682. DEFICIENCY OF VorownsEn OFFICERS. -- The latest returns received at the War Office concerning the proportion of officers commissioned in the Volunteer force up to the beginning of the present i month, show that though the total s greater than it was a few weeks back, it is still far below the proper complement. In Lancashire the deficiency is still considerable; no less than 230 officers being at the time indicated requisite to complete the es- tablishment. Local corps are deficient as follows: —2nd Engineers (St. Helens), 5; let Volunteer Bat- talion South Lancashire (Warrington), 11: and 2nd Volunteer Battalion South Lancashire (St. Helens), 1. It is hoped that the operations of the increased capitation grant, reducing the -pecuniary liabilities of officers, may tend to reduce the insufficiency of the commissioned ranks. I Nov "QUITE ENGLISH. You KNOW." John Broadhurst, baker, Brook-street, was summoned to Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, to answer a charge of not having his name painted on his cart. —P.C. Boyle said another baker drew his attention to the "fact that the defendant's name was not painted on the cart."-- The name was written in chalk upon one of the shafts. The defendart said this was a piece of spite .on the part of Finch, of Warrington who was in the same trade as himself. On the day in question Finch had followed his (defendant's) two lads into, every shop they went into, trying to prevent them selling. This was a free country, and he thought they should be able to sell where they liked. Finch afterwards tried to," throttle" one of the lads and the 'other he struck and gave a black eye. He (defendant) thought it hardly right ' that out of spite he should be brought up there and put to this expense. It Was not English. (Laugh- ter.)---The Bench remarked that they had nothing to do with a trade grievance, and imposed a fine of 6d. and costs. 10s. 6d. SEPARATION • AFTER A FORTNIGHT'S MARRIED LIFB.—A sad case of domestic infelicity came before the magistrates (Lieut.-Colonel W. W. Pilkington, Alderman T. Cook, and Mr. W. Blinkhorn), at the St. Helens Town Hall. on Monday, when a young man named William Lowe, residing in Chancery- lane, was summoned by his wife Mary, on a charge of deserting her. It appeared that the case was be- fore the court on the 2nd inst., when the parties had only been married a week on the previous Sun- day. The case was then adjourned to see if the parties could come to a settlement. On Monday last the defendant stated that he did not intend to live with his wife. The complainant, Mary Lowe, then gave evidence. She stated that she and the defendant were married at Parr Church six weeks ago. Her husband left her a month ago last Wed- nesday, and had been living at his mother's home. Since the last time they Appeared at court she had seen him three times, and he had promised her 35 per week. He was a miner, and , the first week of their married life he gave her £1 2s 6d as his week's wages.—The Peputy Magistrates Clerk (Mr. DllN't- son) to the defendant: You say you don't want to live with her? Defendant; Yes. I don't want to do so.—The Chairman (Mr. Pilkington) : Why don't ' you wish to live with her ?—The defendant said the reason was that the complainant came crying to their house and made a statement which had proved , to be falso.—The Chairman said he was bound to maintain her.—The defendant said his wages were only 21s 3d in winter time, and he would promise her 3s per week.—The Chairman: If you get mar- ried you have to perform certain obligations.—De- fondant: Yes, and I got married on a mee con- sideration h—The Chairman: Then you bad bette7 pay her 58 a week on a further consideration.—An order for the payment of this amount was then made.

Brock, Wilfred Jannion and James Wainwright, labourers, were charged on remand with having stolen three fowls belonging to Mr. Crosby, Lingley's Green Perm, Sankey. Prosecutor had missed twenty fowls from his premises since the 13th inst., and identi- fied three of them which were found in the posses- sion of the prisoners. The two men were handed over to the Warrington county police. Yesterday they were brought before Mr. Edward Greenall, at the Occasional Court, and were remanded to Newton Petty Sessions. JUDGMENT IN MIR Sr. ifiCLENB PA.TENT CASE.— In the Chancery Division: of the High Court of Justice on Wednesday afternoon, Mr. Justice Keke- wich delivered judgment in this case. The action was brought by Messrs. A. G. Kurtz and Co., chemi- cal manufacturers, earring on business at St. Helens, to restrain the defendants, Messrs. I'. Spence and Sons, chemical manufacturers, carrying on business at Miles Platting, near Manchester, from. infring'mgthe plaintiffs' letters patent for the re- moval of iron from sulphate of alumina, which is extensively used for fixing dyes on cloth, and in calico printing and paper staining. Mr. Justice Kekewich pointed out that it was said that Mr. Kynaston, whose invention the plaintiffs used, was not the real discoverer, but that Peter Spence was the first and true inventor. There arose the ques- tion of fact, whether Messrs. Spence, on the one hand, or Kynaston, on the other, was the first and trae inventor of the particular method for which the lett3rs patent were granted. He came to the conclusion upon the evidence that Messrs. Spence discovered the invention before Kynaston. He was further of opinion that 31essr5. Spence had not given the public the information the public were entitled to in the specification with regard to the two methods. The result was that lie gave judg- ment for the plaintiffs, and granted an injunction restraining the continuance of the threats, and ordered the def3ndants to pay the costs of the action.

div.head: CHRISTMASTIDE AT WIDNES AND RUNCORN.
div.p: CHRISTMASTIDE AT WIDNES AND RUNCORN.

The inhabitants of the twin towns of the Mersey ; will enter into the approaching Christmas festivi- ties with more than their usual ardour and enjoy- ment. Both Widnes and Runcorn are greatly depen- dent upon the chemical trade for an existence, and a depression in the staple industry causes a corres- pondent gloom and feeling of uncertainty amongst i the working classes, who form the entire population I of both towns. Five years ago trade was at a very ' low ebb, and there was misery and want in numer- ous humble homes in Widnes, which the charitably- disposed endeavoured to alleviate. In fact at that time there were a thousand, or nearly approaching that number, of dwelling-houses without a tenant, . a state of things too palpably indicative of strai- tened circumstances to need further demonstration. During the past two years, however, there has been a most welco-ne tmward tendency in the several indus- tries of the loca'tv, ana this has become more pro- noanced vitbia the p.ist few months. At the present time there is scarcely a house in VVidness that is empty, and owners of property have taken advantage of the great demand to increase the rents in wt..; many instances. There is, too, a prospect of a fe-..,her increase of population In a few months, when it is anticipated that the' Broughton Copper Cpmpany in Ditton-road v,ill have opened their immense weal, and com- menced the manufacture of their special roes. On the Cheshire side, of course, a feeling of cheerfulness and hopeirnoss is caused by the operations of the , Manchester Ship Canal Company. Aithough it is unlikely that the actual making of the canal will be commenced withim the limits of the town for some months to come owing to the engineering difficulties

that wig there have to be contended m ah, work has been commenced at the "Big Field" in the township of Nor- ton. At this spot about 150 men are at work clearing off from the line of tbe proposed canal the brushwood aria trees, and the erection of *a. N :llage of huts preparatory to commencing cuttin7 operatiorys. At Moss-side, Moor, upwards of half a mile of rarway metals have been laid, and an engine is on the spot, titted up for working. The necessary war,ons are expected to be on the ground in a few days. From thcoe few senteaces it will be seen that there is evelj-thing to encourage and little to depress the people of Widnes aad Runcorn. That the tradesmen were in a more speculative and hopeful mood was seen an "Show night" (Thursday), iv:len every shop was bright with the Maze of gas and stocked with seasonable articles of every conceivable kind. Groat interest was taken in the display by both old and young, and until a late hour the streets were thronged with sightseers.

div.head: RUNCORN PUBLICAN IN TROUBLE.
div.p: A RUNCORN PUBLICAN IN TROUBLE.

At Runcorn Petty Sessicns, on Monday, John Coxhill, landlord of the Greenway Vaults, Greenway-road, was summoned for keeping his house open eluting prohibited hours, and Samuel Buxton and Launcelot Buxton were charged with being upon the premises. Mr. P. A.. Lakedefended. —P.S. Woolley deposed that at seven minutes past eleven on the night of the 12th December he saw the defen- dants Buxton walk into the Greenway Vaults.. and at ten minutes past he followed them. Healed Mrs. Cox- hill if she knew what time it was, and she replied "Yes, it is two minutes past eleven." He replied "It is ten minutes past and you ought to have the house closed." The Buxtons then drank their liquor up and walked out of the house.—Outside Samuel. Buxton said he had thoeght it was too late to get a drink, but seeing the doer open h. walked in and got one.—P.C. Kettle cor- robonded.—Mr. Lake stated that on the Wednesday be- fore this offence was alleged to have been committed Mr. Coxhill fell through a trap door, which had been left opent and damaged his foot badly. He was in bed at the time in question, oral for some days afterwards, and was still unable to leave the house. In consequence of this injury he was incapable of looking after his busi- ness, and the house was in charge of his wife and son. The main question turned ur on what the time really was. The Sergeant stated he kept his watch by the own Hall clock, which was proverbial forbeingveryunc 4. in. er4 He should prove by witnesses that it was about a to and a halflo eleven o'clock when the men ent he house, and only two minutes past eleven when the con- stables appeared on the scene. Mr. Lake pointed out that Corhill had held a license for twcnty years, and during that time had never had a single charge biought against him. Witness hang been called to prove the advocate's statements, the Bench fined Coxhv'l 20s and costs lOs 6d, and the other defendants 10s, and costs lOs 6d, each.

div.head: TILE 3LECROSVOPE.
div.p: TILE 3LECROSVOPE.
THE MANY PUZZLING SECRETS REVEALED BY THIS WONDEII.II3L INSTI3.I7MENT.

No medical man of skill and ability considers his study, at the present time, complete unless it con- tains a first-class microscope. This wonderful in- strument, by its marvellous power, makes clear to our eyes a world of which, prior to its inveation, we knew nothing. Its introduction into medicine is only of late years, and has been Mainly brought about by the competi4on of practitioners in their endeavour to find some aid that would enable them to detect the pres- ence of disease when hidden or masked ; to diagnose with greater accuracy, and so secure that prominence in their profession upon which their fame and emoluments rest. But its use has been more particularly applied to the examining of the fluids of the body Ito determine the state of the kidneys and decide if the latter are in a state of diseses, and if so, its stage. It has already been the means of saving many a life in foreshadcrvring the advent of that stealthy and fatal disease to which Dr. Richard Bright gave his name, and which, prior to the introduction of "Warner's SAFE Cute," was • always re- garded as incurable. In all the history of the microscope its use was never so prevalent, its study never prosecu- ted with so much vigour, as it is to-day, and science, through its means, is ever revealing something fresh and new in relation to its powers. For instance, a noted physician and German scholar has recently discovered that by its aid the presence off a tumour forming in the system can be detected, and if certain appearances ate visible it is proof positive that the tumour, or growth, is of a malignant character. Uric acid, which is a rank poison, is one of the substances which arise from des- tructive waste of our body, and must be thrown off daily, or we die. Now, before we understood the micro- scope it was impossible by any means at our command. to know what was being passed out dour body,or from whence it caine; and one great, benefit which this instru- ment has conferred upon humanity is in the relief of headaches, inalai4e, indisposition, and other diseases, which are now known to be caused by the retention of uric acid in the body. When an analysis of the fluid is made by a micro-chemical examination this substance can be traced in its proper quantity, and when the pro- per remedy is applied relief is soon secured. the curebeing effected almost immediately, ' This uric acid, in nine cases out of ten, is responsible for all the ailments from which we suffer; its retention pro- duces serious disorders, and the diseases which it causes may be treated, and formerly were treated, without avail, for they can never be cured unless the uric acid is removed. This same uric acid has another sin to answer for. It may be passed out of the kidneys, but from some inability the bladder is unable to excrete it. It is re- tained there, collects, increases, Isec,orries aggluthsated, and forms stone, by a chemical process of -which we know nothing at present, and then there is no relief except the terrible operation of cutting and crushing. From this it will be seen how necessary it is to keep the kidneys in proper working order, to enable them to perform their ceaseless labours of ridding the system of the waste materials. The tendeney of all kidney disease is towards Bright's disease, and if it is neglected this is sure to result. Dieease of the kidneys cannot be fully recog- nised without the aid of the microscope : not only has it giversthe physician this information, but it has revealed the universal prevalence of his fatal disease. It has changed the diagnosis, and, fact, the entire treatment of diseases as laid down by the old authors Persons who a few years ago were supposed to have died fm general debility, dropsy, paralysis; rheumatism,. appoplaxy, Sm., are now known to have actually died from diseased kidneys. Had there been no disease of these organs, had the uric acid been carried out, the chances are that the effects from which they ultimately succumbed would not have existed. • As the world becomes better acquainted with the importance of the kidneys, as shown by the microscope, there is greater alarm spread through the tsSinmunities concerning their waif ate; and well it should be so, for, directly or indirectly, diseased kidneys are the Cease of more deaths than any other form of disease. As we said before, medical science has been unabt LS Cel cope with this disease, and neither homSathics nor allopathics are prepared with a Cilre for deranged kidneys; and all the world has long since recognised, and many medical men who sse without bias and with- out prejudice liberal-Minded, and anxious to cure, admit and prescribe' "Warner's SAFE Cure" as a specific for all diseases of the kidneys. Formerly the true cause of death was only discovered after death, and many a victim has passed away him pneumonia consumption, and kindred diseases, when a post-mortem examination has shown a rotten kidney, which was the first cause of the break-down. To-day the microscope shows us in the water whether it is dangerous and where the trouble lies, allowing the medical man to treat it -.properly, and so enable the patient to escape premiture death. It is the duty of every medical man to examine the urine of every patient that comes under his care. Dr. Tyler says it is necessary to do so even when dyspepsia only is the trouble, because the retention of uric acid is the cause of the irritation of the stomach. The eminent Dr. Graves said that he wanted his epitaph," Dr. Graves, he fed fevers." And says Dr. Thomas Ware, appreciating the great im- portance of this subject, "I want my epitaph to read, Dr. Thomas Ware, he examined urine. • Warner's SAFE Cure,' like the microscope, was found out by a layman outside .the medical code. The uni- versal testimony of our friends and neighbours shows it to be alone the remedy for all diseases of the kidneys, their prevention and cure. Their statements are suf- ficient explanation and endorsement of its extraordinary growth, and conclusive proof that it is, perhaps,.the most munificent remedy known to the medical world since the microscope revealed to us the all-important nature of the organs which this medicine is specifically designed te benefit.—Health, Sept. 30.

'THE SMALL-PDX dt sAditee Hameats. The Ctene read a letter from the Local Government Board in which they called attention to a letter they had received from Dr. tiornall in reference to the small-pox cases at Sankey Bridges, and asked for the observations of the Rural Sanitary Authority on the subject. He then read Dr. Goma letter, a copy of whichwas enclosed. It stated "that they (the Local Government Board) would see by an annexed newspaper cutting that acaseof small pox had occurred in the Warrington Rural Sanitary District just outside the Warrington Municipal boundary, for which he was medical officer of health. They would be wen aware that the contiguity of the two districts made it imperative that most stringent measures should be taken to prevent its introduction into this borough,' and he wrote to complain that a rural district should be allowed to handicap an important borough which was doing all in its power to arrest the dissemination of zymotic disease. The case he referred to was intreduced from Sheffield and had been wandering about the dis- trict for about three weeks without medical attendance, and that morning (December sth) another practitioner (Dr. Joseph) informed him that he was, the previous day, called to a mild Case of smallpox in the same neighbourhood, and that no attempt at isolation was being made." The Clerk added that this was a matter for the Rural Sanitary Authority, but with regard to this correspondence their medical officer (Dr. Sephton) wrote to say "that every precaution was being taken to prevent the spread of the disease. The case was isolated, as far as possible, in an upper room, with only one attendant, disinfectants freely used, part of the clothing and bedding had al- ready been destroyed, and full instructions had been given as to going out and exposure in public places. In the second case, viz., William Allman, Richardson'e-row, Sankey Bridges, isolation was impossible, as there were only a living room and one bedroom for father and three sons. These houses were back to back houses, and no ventilation through them. They were using all the precautions they could in this case, which was a very mild one. They could say that in neither case had they the power to remove, and the patients refused to go into hospital, and they did not come under the 124th or 91st section of the Public Health Act. They might call upon the vaccination officer, through the Board of Guardian.s, to see that vaccination and re-vaccination in the in- infected neighbourhood was fully carried out. He would write to the Local Government Board respecting the cases, and give them full particulars." The CLIME said with regard to the last part of this letter, that the vacci- nation officer of the Board had done all he could in com- pliance with the regulations .—The CHAIRMAN said that the matter which occurred to his mind was that if the patients referred to had been. willing to be removed, there would be no hospital to take them to; they had no accommodation in the workhouse.—Mr. Gees:sew said they had nee power to take them into the workhouse. It was the place of the Rural Sanitary Authority to find accommodation for patients in case of infectious disease. —Mr. Joze.ify remarked that if there was an outbreak of infectious disease in a street partly in the borough and partly in the rural district, there was power to remove a patient from a house in the borough, while there was no power to remove a case in the rural district, although the house in the borough and that in the rural district might immediately adjoin each other.—The CLERK said that in case of a fire outside the borough the corporation. were perfectly willing to allow their fire engine to go to it, and they afterwards sent in a bill of the costs, but the cor- poration dealt in a different manner with the somewhat analogous case of an outbreak of infectious disease. The Rural Sanitary Authority and the• Board of Guardians had always been prepared to enter into a similar arrange- ment with the Borough Authority with regard to cases of disease, but in this instance the corporation insisted that the Rural Sanitary Authority should not only pay a certain sum for the maintenance of the patients, but also a permanent yearly sum. He did not see why they should adopt one arrangement with regard to the fire engine and another with regard to the hospital, for there would be far greater danger to the people of Warrington from an outbreak of small-pox outside the borough than .from a fire at some farm building.—Mr. RATCLIFFE said at Newton they paid £lO4 a year to the Warrington hos- pital and les a week for, the maintenance of any patient they might have there. As far as Newton was concerned, they had no difficulty with Warrington; they paid man- fully, and he thought the Rural Sanitary Authority ought to enter into a similar arrangement and pay the charges, as Newton did.—Mr. DA.RETSHIIIH said the Rural Sanitary Authority formerly had an arrangement with the Warrington Corporation for the use of the hospital, 'by which they paid £l3O a year and les a week for any patient they might have in. They had withdrawn from that arrangement, and he hoped they might never enter into such an arrangement again. For his part he should prefer to have a cottage hospital in any part of the Rural Sanitary Authority's district that might need it. It was enough to kill a country patient to bring him into War- rington even if there was nothing much the matter with him. (Laughter.)—Mr. OWEN said that when they had the agreement referred to by Mr. Darbyshire with the Corporation, the Corporation would not undertake to find accommodation if they required all the hospital themselves.—Mr. GREENING said the Warrington hospital was not built with the intention r>f filling it with country people that might be afflicted with infectious disease. It was built purely and simply to isolate cases that oc- curred in the borough. It was the country districts who sought the assistance of the Corporation; they were never asked and they were not asked at the present time. It was perfectly right for the Rural Sanitary Authority to discontinue paying the £l3O a year and les a week, but if the Rural Sanitary Authority allowed small-pox I and fever or other infectious diseases to be in Qoe proximity to the borough, the proper course fee borough, when it was in such danger, was to thy' authorities to compel the Rural Sanitary Au9' build a hospital of its own. He hoped the Rut Authority would build a hospital of their ev they would maintain it in a proper and effio He thought the Authority would find belle I very much older that they would be compel a hospital, or, as Mr. Darbyshire suggested, take some premises which could be converted into a hospital.—ThA CHAIRMAN said that any arrangement they might make with the borough would not remove all their difficulties, a; the borough would only undertake to :accommodate their patients when they had room in their hospital. But in the cases of smallpox that had been referred to in that discussion, the patients were not willing to be re- moved.—The matter then dropped.

BY HENRY WHITEIAM. Your readers will scarcely desire thttt I should occupy your space with anything like a detailed account of the country through which the traveller passes on his way from New York to San Francisco.. Before he leaves the vessel he has a foretaste, on his way from Sandy Hook to the dock, of•what nature is going to unfold to his wondering gaze. On each side, tier above tier, and almost lost in rich foliage, stand beautiful and picturesque villa residences. Nature has done her share, and in this country man has helped her. It is in the city all seems to go wrong. Before we mix with the madding crowd, how- ever, allow me to describe Castle Gardens. As emigrants, we had to stay on the vessel all night. Restrictions of a most stringent character are used to prevent the steerage passengers from landing. Intermediate and saloon passengers may do pretty.. nearly as they like; vaccinatedlor unvaccinated they may land, but every man, woman, and child, wile happens to lack dimes and dollar, s must bare, his, or her arm, to show the mark. Lacking this mark, the doctor immediately performs the operation. The emigrant having landed, then commences his troubles His luggage is tumbled out of the hold as if it was so much rubbish. It is no use marking it "this side up,' out it goes, if the boxes are whole. More than one strong box did I see smashed all to match wood, and the contents spread about. Every one running here and there seeking their posses- sions, all is a perfect Babel, and the poor emigrant is fairly bewildered when he falls into the Custom House officer's hands to be still more dazed. Boxes that are nailed, and boxes that are locked, bags that are sewed up, and bags that are tied up. all must be laid open to his profane hands before arriving within the secret and labyrinthine precincts of the famous Gardens. Here the emigrant answers all ggestions as to what he has been, whet he is, and what he is going to bp, and if all is not satisfactory, woe be to Wm. This troublesonto work all gone through, the traveller is at liberty to take his first look at. the, greatest city on the American continent. My own opinion is that New York is about the dirtiest, worst paved, and, munici- pally speaking, the worst governed city in the world. Of course I had but a few hours there, yet I think three or four hours spent in Broadway and two or three other of the principal streets entitles me to say so much. Everyone seems to be bent on gaining the almighty dol- lar. Personal comfort, or the convenience of foot-pas- sengers is altogether secondary. Express men and wag- gons like ships tako precedence over all else; hurry,' scurry, oh! how thankful we all were to get once more on the ferry en route for Jersey, and the train that was to bear us over the continent to the Pacific coast. Once inside the train, believe me, we knew how to ap- preciate the well upholstered seats. Whatever America lacks she certainly is not behind in the comfort she pro- vides for her travellers. And to us, who had gone through a Pair amount of hardship, having for nearupon three weeks been like the Son of Mannot knowing where to lay either our poor heads or our poor bodies, we vrel- corned the comfortable railway road carriage. On Tues- day morning the 15th November we left the ship; the same evening we left behind us all the din and noise of New York. Travelling in the night time is not satisfac-, tory to the sight-seer. To be told at various times dur- ing the night that you are passing through some famous town is calculated to make one angry, yet it has its com- pensatory features. For instance, I stood outside the carriage, on the platform, while crossing the bridge which spans the Susquehannah river; no balustrades, not the slightest attempt at railings, or protection of any kind, the railroad just tho width of the train. Oh what a shock, and how near the end seems to be! A crank, a bolt, the slightest hitch and over the dizzy edge we should go. But on we went, tearine a-head through the darkness, scores of times rounding the dizzy precipice in I r blissful ignorance of our hair-breadth escapes. ' Leaving the lower fiat lands of the Eastern States, , we began to ascend what, I think, are called the Blue Ridge Mountaias. Then we gain our first experience of what railway travelling really is. Winding up a tortu- ous and very uneven railway track, we seem in danger at times of taking leave of the engine. The fore part of the carriage would dive down as if determined, to ex- 1 ploro the lower depths, pull up again, and we should find after a series of jerks, jumps, and bumps, that all was right, and we were still tearing ahead to an alti- tude sufficiently high to satisfy any reasonable member of the Alpine Club. Along the route, which is one of a succession of clearances, it is noticed that nearly all the new settlers are of German and Dutch origin, whose -lives must be passed in loneliness and privation; but this is preferred to the patriarchal and despotical system which new obtains in Germany, and which, I am sorry to say, a Conservative party is labouring so hard to bring about in England. Chicago is the first largo city we reach, and, after a 1 good meal and a good wash, we ramble for a couple of i hours over the city. It is a splendid place, with fine noble-looking buildings, and not the least sign of the' recent conflagration to be seen. Attentive niggers prove before you leave the city how well they have pro- fited by association with the white man in the art of ex- tracting coin from your pockets; it makes me glad to get seated once more in the car en route for Council Bluff. All heavy luggage has to be checked and re-checked several tunas, as in the journey from East to West the traveller has to change and travel along the line; of vari- ous companies. I may say that the ttain stops each evening for twenty minutes to enable the, traveller to rush out, generally in the dark, and And a bakery, where he meets with all sorts of prices and every degree of roguisnness. To anyone coming out, I should advise that a thorough knowledge of the American system of coinage be gained, as the purveyors on the road will resort to any device to gain possession of the god they worship—the almighty dollar. I could, of course, fill your paper with descriptive matter, gained by actual observation, or culled from a volume before me. The scenery through which we passed was simply awful in its grandeur; miles upon miles of sandy plains, through which the emigrant, before the track was laid, had to make his weary way; snowcapped mountains that towered up to the clouds, through can- yons, whose steep sides shut out the light of the sun; all these sights kept us, like "Alice inwonderland,"in a state of intense astonishment. When we reached Ogden, the stopping place in Utah, we were almost inclined to respect the debauched mind and persevering will of the early Mormon settlers, who had risked so much to gain such a worthless object. Al- low me hero to say that all the Gentiles in Mormon land are of one opinion respecting its peculiar religion; the girls they " import " are simply used for two purpose*, slavery and lust. Rounding the great Salt Lake and an immense desert which surrounds it, we reached, on the Sunday, an im- mense level platform, on which the cars stopped, and some scores of passengers turned out to hunt the Jack Rabbit. Soon gun and pistol were heard at work, and fine fun we had for nearly an hour. I should say that the only vegetation to be seen in these trackless desert is the sage bush, which grows in immense quantities,and quite scents the air. On we go again, descending now past Humbolt, where we begin to see the redskins, who seem a poor, lost, beggarly lot, living no one knows how, until we begin to ascend the Rocky Mountains, and pass through long snow sheds, built to keep the snow off the track. From hero to Sacramento, which we reached ,at midnight, and then we see little more until we reach San Francisco, after a railroad journey that has taken just a week to accomplish. Sleeping at night in emigrant- sleeping cars, and getting our food as we could, you can imagine how glad I was to find a friend waiting for me, he having come down each day for more than a week past, daily expecting us. I shall in my next have something to say respecting Mrs. Parker's letters, which have appeared in various English papers, and which, I see, have already provoked a discussion in your own colums. I beg your readers to accept her letters with caution. When she writes of San Francisco she writes in ignorance. I have had only a `ortnight here, and if I never believed when at home in sit, Jean now say with certainty that it exists on the
Ific slope. get your papers all right. lam sorry to say ife has been in bed, very ill, ever since we arrived, taken ill on the way.

WIDNISS T. Ecams.--Considerable 'disappointment was experienced by. the supporters of the Eccles club on Saturday at the result of their match with the "chemi- cals.", Last year, when Widnes went to Eccles they suffered 'defeat, and special precautions were taken on Saturday to ensure a repetition of the dose, three good players , having been secured from the neighbouring Barton club; but it was to no purpose, as the iisitors won comfortably by a goal and eight minor to one try and two minors. Playing uphill in the first half, Widnes pressed immediately, and scored a touchdown. The. home team retaliated by. scoring a dead ball, after re- peated attseks had bc9n mule by the Widnesians on their citadel; a,ricl (hon. Parkinson -secured a try for the visitors, as the result of some smart passing by Woods, Kiddie, and Sampson. Morris kicked a fine goal. Drury scored a good try for Eccles in the second half, but,failed at goal. Widnes had hard lines repeatedly, crossing the line three times; having tries disallowed to Hardnian, J. Bingham, and Gandy. The game thus closed as above stated, Teams :—Widnes ; S. Bingham, back; Plutnpton, Parkinson, and Morris, three-quarter backs; Farrell and Wilkinson, half backs; Smith (captain), Headman, Kiddie, J. Bingham, Woods. Bather, Gandy, Sampson, and Pennington, forwards. Eccles : Foote, back; Skelly, Chambers, and Daly, throe- quarter backs; Balsa euid Drury, half backs; Wood- head, Evans, Nunn, Holt, Pickup, Moores, Wolfonden, Britch, and Holsworth, forwards. RUNCORN v. BROUGHTOX RANGHs9.—These two clubs met on the ground of the _former on Saturday, 2,00413 spectators lining the enclosure. The visitors came with a strong team; while for the home club Cavrloy, Broady, and Wright, were absent, but. notwithstanding, a grand game resulted, the Rangers getting the verdict by two tries and two touehdowas to two minors. Broughton kicked off at 3.10, at once invading the home 25, Riley transfer- ring operations to centre. Then M‘Gotran took play to Runcorn's qmarters, where several scrimmages wero formed, Woods having eventually to save. The Rangers, after the drop-out, had to act on the defensive' the ball being kicked into touch at their goal line, and from the line-out a pack was formed in front of goal, but ,Barlow caused the home teem to retire, winding up his movp- ment by gaining a try, Boyle failing at the place. Hughes took the leather from mid-field to the visitor's 25 flag, M'Gowan upsetting his Calculations,. and Run- corn had to retire to the centre; but the home backs dis- played some fine passing, tactics, and when the whiffle announced half-time the game was located in Broughton's 25. No time being wasted in changing over, Runearn set the oval in motion, Barlow replying. The home for- wards worked-the leather to tho Rangers' 25 flag, when H. Hughes was spoiled from getting a try by Boyle, and the anxlet7 of the visitors was quickly removed by the leather being transferred to mid-field. Speakman now dashed off, bul-SqUires checked his onward movement, the last-named player dribbling to the home 25, when the bail was kicked dead. The spectators now applauded Wainwright for A grand run, his effort being rewarded by the Rangers conceding a touchdown. The visitors, with the aid of M4Gowan, caused a scrimmage in Run- corn 25, and Boyle (full back). who had come well up the field, getting posSession of the leather, gained a try, but failed at the place. The Rangers confirmed to hold the upper hand for a time, when at length Speakman caused them to act on the defensive, and eventually compelled them to touch down. The only feature from this point to the finish was the concession of a minor point by the home team, M'Gowan heing accountable for this. There was very little to choose between the forwards in the packs; while for individual efforts Boyle, M'Growan, and Barlow, for Broughton, showed best form • and T. Davies, H. Hughes, W. Hughes, P. and W. Riley, and. Wainvrright, were moat conspicuous for Runcorn. Teams :—Broughton Rangers: A. Boyle, back; Poole, J. M`Gowan, and J. Robertson, three- quarter backs • W. Edge and W. Wood, half backs; A. Stott, R. Hughes, Barlow, F. Atkinson, T. Squires, C. Skidmore, S. E. . Moxon. and Tune, for- wards. Runcorn: T. Harrison,Voods, • back; T. Davies, H. Speakman, and W. Biley,three-quarter backs; H. Hughes and H. Andrews, half backs; W. Hughes. W. Faulkner, J. Lewis, J. Burns, J. Bowyer, G. Wainwright, J. Gatloy, P. Riley, and J. Clarke, forwards. WARRINGTON V. WKRNETH.

The first-named club having in open date on Saturday Werneth filled up the vacancy, and brought their best team to try conclusions with Warrington,. who wore without Massey,' Fair. Turner, and B. Dillon. There was only a poor attendance of spectators, consequent on the unfavourable state of the weather; and two twenty- fives having been agreed upon, Fitton started the game from mid-field, tho home skipper (Barnes) returning to centre. The Warrington forwards overpowered their opponents, and took the oval to the line. From a suc- ceeding scrimmage Warren endeavoured to get over, but the safe tackling of the visitors prevented this, relieving to the quarter flag. Barnes negatived by a timely kick, and Speakman with a grand effort almost got in, the greasy state of the ball however, prevented him; and to this cause must be attributed the fact that no major point could be scored. From a return by Tomlinson, Ashton made his mark in a favourable position, but Bandies failed to notch the coveted goal, Coape running the ball out. The game raged chiefly on the visitors' lines, and Speakman again threatened the visitors' goal, but slipped when scoring seemed a certainty. Bandies was to the fore with a neat run and pats to Appleton, who gained a little ground. The Werneth men were forced back, and some neat dribbling by the Warring ' - tonians headed by Littlewood and Appleton, ended in the ball going In touch close to the corner flag. Wood relieved the pressure by a good dribble to midfield, but a pass by Speakman across tki -Appleton ended in the latter almost gettin, in. Povey threaded his way through the pack, and Speakman got the leather away, parted to !James, who transferred to Jolley, the latter being held on the lines. A minor was shortly afterwards conceded. The drop out brought little relief to tho Wer- neth men. and Jolley was about this time applauded for some dashing runs. Speakman gave Jolley a chance but the fates were against him. The last named was again to the fore with a sterling run and pass to Barnes, who lost possession when crossing the line. From now to the call of half-time, a complete siege was made on the Werneth citadel, but no addition to the score was ob- tained, and when the whistle was blown the Warring- tonians had scored one minor to nil. Randle.' re-started, and a poor return being made, a scrimmage wits formed ,in the Werneth twenty-five. Exchange kicking by Ap- pleton and Simpson gained ground for the visitors, but Jolley got away, only to find his way blocked by Buck- ley. Davies spoiled some passing by the opposing backs. but Shirt relieved to mid-field. W. 'Dillon, Rigby, and Hayes were instrumental in taking the leather to the Wemoth line. Simpson put in a good run, but Appleton brought him to grass. Warren effected a wide pass to Appleton, but Simpson safely held him. The game was exceedingly rough during this half, and the play that took place calls for little comment. Each side strove hard to obtain a major point but without avail, and after 50 minutes' play the whistle was blown with no addition to the score—Warrington one minor, Waned' nil. The game was not an enjoyable one, and certainly the same form was not displayed as was the case on the provims Saturday against Dewsbury. Sp!.alunan was the best back on the field, anti Jolley put in some ster7 ling work. Appleton and Warren rendered useful work at times. Of the forwards Littlewood, W. Dillon, and Randles were the pick. The fnnowing were the teams— , Warrington : Full back, Nevins; three-quarter backs, Jolley, Barnes (captain), and Appleton; half-backs, Warren and Speakman • forwards, Ashton, W. Dillon, Davies, Donohue, Littlewood, Hayes Povey, Bandies, and Rigby. • Werneth : Full hack, Tomlinson;' ' three- quarter backs, Shirt, Coape, and Simpson ; half-backs, Hayne and Buckley; forwards, Fitton, A Wood, J Wood,- Kent, J Whyatt, it Whyatt, Simpson, Shortrid,ge, and Hankinson.

div.p: :CE
- BY THE WAY.

•In the mooting between Warrington and Werneth on Saturday, the spectators were not favoured with an ex- hibition of the highest style of play. The Werneth players seemed to rely more upon . force than skill, and as a. result thescrimmagas at times degenerated into a more or less rou,gli scuffle: On the other hand it must be confessed that the hoine teamwere far ,from displaying their highest form, either forward or behind. With% all their faults, however, they were distinctly superior to their antagonists, and it was only their adversoluck which prevented them from notching a winning' point in the-first part•of the game. • -•-- -- - ----r- - Christmastide (is Nicely to afford plenty of entertain- ment for admirers Of football in Warrington. To-day, there will be an encounter betereen the home 'team and Oldham, and on Mbnday Barnes' followers will, again meet the Wigan team on the Wilderspool ground. Earlier in the day on Monday the final tie in the West Lanca- shite Junior competition will be played' on 'the War- rington ground between Widnes Recreation and Wood- man Rovers. • , . It is becoming evident that Runcorn will have to pull themselves together if hey are to maintain the brilliant reputation they so justly earned last season. • Saturday saw them akiin defeated, Broughton Rangers on this occasion dome tho needful. Of course it is only fair to state that in several instineee victory has been missed by a hair's breadth as the @ap- ing is, and had., ,Iroodei, , been • equal to 'his , position at full back_ on Saturday, the -popular wearers 'of .the green,-would not have retired de: festal. On each occasion the Rangers scored Woods mulled the ball in a mannor Vitally inexplicable to his many admirers: but we trestle will be in his old form to-day at Dewsbury. The first try was obtained after a very palpable'" pass forward," a fact admitted by several of the , visitors afterwards, and upon what grounds the • referee (Mr. Roger Wilceck) ig- nored the appeal is unknown. With the excel:), tion of Woods, the backs -played a fine game, W. Riley cspciallr distinguishing himself by his clever kicking and saving; and in the second half Speak- man and Davie§ treated the spectators to a reingrkably smart piece of passing wbich Unfortunately was without reCult: As to the forwards, it was pleasing to notice that W. Dughee was, as usual, working like a horse; whilst P. Riley, Faulkner, and Wainwight were all to the fore, but there is no gainsaying that as a whole the forwards do not play with the dash and. combination on the loose that was once their boast and the pride of their supporters. Widnes had again an "easy thing on" on Saturday when they eave Eccles their quietus to the tune of one goal and eight minors to one try and two miners. Tho game was much more ene-sided that the scoed would in- dicate, Widnes having no less than three tries disalloWed. It is a pity they have not higher game to fly at. Whatever may be the distination *of the senior ' cup, the West Lancashire Junior Club is-very likely to &idea , resting place. at Widnes through the operations ef the Widnes Recreatihn. This team will on Monday meet Woodman Rovers, Wigan, in the final tio at Warrington, and the Recreation are the favourites."

I.Tivr Adventures of tittle Man-Chester" is the 'title oi an illustrated childron's souvenir of, the Manchester Ex- hibition. It is published by Messrs. 'Abel Hey Wood. and Son Manchester, and it is beautifully printed in colours.' The drawings are by" E.. Ellen Houghton," the gifted wife 'of Mr. IL N.! Houghton; Warrington. Mrsi libughton shows herself clever and fanciful, and she has a quick , eye for the humours of the situation. "Little , Man-Chester" is sure to be' popular with those Who want a pleasant reminder of a pleaSant Exhibition. " The Lover and other Papers of' Steele and Addison" is the title of the December issue of the Camelot series published by Mr. Walter Scott: The volume is edited by Mr. Walter Lewin, who gives an interesting account, of the career of Steel% and of the various literary vontureS with which he WilB a,sc.Ociaied. Like much of Steele's writing, "The Lover" is very readable at thiS day •' it displays a genuine regard for woman ; and abounds in .quaint fancies and . delightful anecdotes.' Addison's papers from the S' Spectator" on Milton's "'Paradise Lost" are also re-produced.' They were justly held in high esteem at the time they were written, and will still be read with great interest by the 'Student of literse ture. "The Life of Tobias George Smollett " appears this. month among the Great Writers. It is from. the pen of Mr. David Hannay, who blends just sufficient criticism with his statement of facts to guide the reader irr coming to a sound judgment as to the character and genius of 'Smollett. The author of "Roderick. Rai:dont, "Pore- -grin° Pickle," ~" Ferdinand Count Fathom'," and "Humphrey Clinker" will alWays have a host Of ad- mirers who will appreciate such a life as that before us. Those too, who know Smollett only through his history, of England will not unnaturally desire to learn something of his own personal history. Amongst the Canterbury Poets, also published by Sir, ,Walter Scott, we have the first instalment of Milton's I works by the issue of "Paradise Lost." It makes a goodly and handsome shilling volume, with the tolerably, full biographical notice by Mr. John Bradshaw, It will be followed at an early date by "Samson Agon- I istes," Minor Poems, &c. It is to be hoped, too, that there will be an /95120 of selections of his prose woks; for Milton was as great a master of prose as of verse. Dryden's epigram as it appeared under the in of. Milton in the fourth edition of his works n 1688, is given; and, as it may be new to some of our readers, we reproduce it : Three Poets in three distant ages born, s Greece, Italy, and England did adorn; r The lust in loftiness of thought surpassed ; The neat in majesty; in both the last. The force of nature could no further go; To make a third she joined the Other two, Messrs. Griffith, Farron, & Co., London, are issuing I two handbooks, at sixpence, Which are likely to be vory, aereptable. They are both recreation handbooks for teachers and scholare,..one being for "Boys' Crames," and the other for "Girls' Games. They are edit ela by E. P. Bourne, and it is evident that great care has been taken to make the handbooks complete. The index shows a surprising number of indoor and outdoor games. Some of the games are, of course, common to both sexes: The explanations are clear and concise, and diagrams are made use of where required. Cassell's Miniature Cyclopcodia, which is being pub- lished in six parts, at sixpence each, is likely to be in great demand. There are over 100 two-column pages in each pelt ; aud by the use of a series of abbreviated symbbls an 4normous amount of information is crowded into each page. The illustrations are excellent, and we confidently recommend the work. ' The second part of "The Dictionary of English His- tory," published by Messrs. Cassell, will make the , reader warm towards the prospect of possessing the , complete work which will be finished in 17 sixpenny ' parts. It is a capital idea to prepare such a book of re- ference ; it will save a great amount of time in many I eases. Writers have sometimes to hunt rather more than they like to confirm a fact in history; they vrill now I have everything they want at their fingers' ends, and the general reader will find this dictionary, unlike some, , an interesting companion. I The Christmas Number of 'Harper's Magazine is as full lof good things as an egg is full of meat. Every article, 'story, and poem, 6 illustrated. "Old Garden Flowers," by -Mr. F. W. Burbidge, has no 'less than eleven illus- trations. Mr. T. B. Aldrich contributes a dramatic , poem—" Pauline Paulovna." It is quite Shakespearean in some of its touches. There is a farce, "Five o'clock Tea," and a comsdietta, "Shot through the head," a poem by Freed, "The Vicar," and several interesting stories. An article by Mr. G. F. Kunz on "Precious Stones in the United States," is accompanied with a very tine plate of gems in colour. The Printer's Handbook," just published by The Chiswick Press, Chancory-lane, London, is a work that i was much required, and s likely, therefore, to be in de- mand amongst printers and workers in 'allied trades. It contains innumerablectrade recipes, hints, and sugges- .tions, relating to letterpress and 'lithographic printing, bookbinding, stationery, engraving, &c. It will be seen that its scope is wide, and we may say of it, after look- lug it carefully through, that there is much in it that would be of use to workmen in almost every branch of industry. For instance, those who have boilers on their premises will find hints as to their preservation, while the ordinary tradesman is told how to proceed in clean- ling gilt frames; and'restoring faded goods in shop win- dows. The handbook has been compiled by Mr. C. T. Jacobi, who has, of course, made the fullest use of the good things in the way of recipes which have been cur- rent for years in trade journals. The tables that are given are exceedingly useful, and will save 'sinters much valuable time, besides ensuring accuracy in vosrk- ing. In these days of technical education, printers, &e., ought to set great store on a work of this kind. It should be added that the handbook is in itself a good specimen of the printer's art. It is to be had at the price of 2s. 6d. nett, or 21. 9d. by- post.
