div.head: ALPINE CHOIR. AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE ALPINE CHOIR. AT WARRINGTON.

Under the etispices of the Warrington Band of Hope Union, 'Professor Andres Alpine choi'r com- menced a three. days' visit to. :Warrington .in the Public Hall, giving one concert on Saturday even- ing. two on Sunday, and one on the evenings of Monday and Tuesday: The choir is 'comprised of nine young ladies, who appear. in Swiss costume, and who very suceeesfully carry out programmes consisting of sacred and secular 'vocal selections, and peformanees on various Musical' instruments, including the gigilira, zither, violin, dulcimer, mandolin, and guitar.: The audiences that have assembled to hear them have been large and appre- ciative. and the members Of the choir on the °tension of each appearance receitred a very flattering wel- come. The chairwas occupied on Saturday even- , big by the Rev. S. Wilkinsoa, vicar, of St.. Paul's, ' who said a few, suitable opening words; and on Monday the Rev. John Yonge, pastor of Wycliffe Congregational Church, presided. In the course of a short speech; he said that they were verk 'glad to ;welcome .the members of the Alpine choir, who had come to help the Band of Hope Union, an institution which was entitled the sympathies of Christian and temperate people in the town. ‘Lle.elaimed on behalf of the Band 9A ,Hope that it had done good service in the cause of teMperance for Wile years. They ,wished to bring that cause prominehtly,Wore the public; and also to get the tnealis to instil noivlife into the ban& of hope connected with the variou.s chnrches and chapels, and hoped by that series of entertainments the Warrinaton Band of Hope might- be able • to do better /The chairman on Tuesday evening 'was the presidentiof the Union, Mr, R. A. Naylor, who remarked that gentleman told him before he came on to the platform that if theyi had brought Jem Smitivorthe great Sulli- van, to the l'ublic Hall, they wouldtha.vw; had a crowded audience. He .did not know whothez that spoke muclP for the tastebf thd 'people, but he thought they got rather, blackguarded in Warrington. , He noticed from the evening newspapers that if anything of a deplorable i character took Place n Warrington, they were held up before the public in the most abominable fashion; and when he told , people living at a distance that he mute. from that town they generally said, "Well, Warrington is a very bad place, accOrding to the' newspapers." They seemed to live in a half-way house between Manchester and Liverpool, and they were shown up very badly by the evening newspapers of those two cities. With regard'to the prize fight, 'he believed that &great struggle had taken place, between the delebrated Jetn.Smith and , some one elsq in Franco, and he was told. that a great number of rrigliShnien wont Over to 'F.rance to witness the combat. He considered that-ail' entertainment of, that. character was of a very brutaiizing tendency— (hear, hear,)—but when they leoked at the programme to be presented that night they wOuld'sec that' it was of an interesting. ZA well as of an elevating character, and his only disappointment wasthat they had not a largo audience. :

div.head: LECTURE AT NEWTON -MU T.W. LEGIT,
div.p: LECTURE AT NEWTON -MU T.W. LEGIT,

. ON. VULQARIA. On Thursday night, in • the Newton Town Hall, Mt. T. W. ,Legh, M.P. for the Newton Division, gave: public lecture oh " My recent travels in Bulgaria and Eastern Europe.'.' The proceeds.were in aid of the old folks' tiea.t fund, And there Was i7yery large and enthnsiastic audience. J•Among thoie present were Mr. T. J. Gillespie, J.P. (who presided), Col: George McCorquodale,J.P., and Mrs.,:ideCorguoclale, Commsnder and Mrs. Royse, R.N., Captain A. D. Seton, Mr. W. F. Gooch, .J.P., Dr. A. -1-Tandyside, Dr. Patterson, Mr. M. Brown-Westhead, Mr. C. 'l3: F. Borron, Mr: George Clarke. Mr. T. H. Pearson.

Rev. W. ,g.. Pugh The Chairman said it. gave him great pleasure to pre- Side on that occasion, and he was sure he echoed the son- tin:tents of every one present when, he said they felt very much inslebted ,to Xr. Legh, foi: so kindly Coming for Ward to give them an ,'aecaunti of his experiences in his Bulgarian travel fi: (Applause.) He congratulated Mr. Legh upon, once, more arriving -safe in England, for from he newspaper repOrts some-. time ago many of his constituents had very grave doubts as to his everartiying safe in. England. Fortunatelyte had done so,„ and they were, glad to see him amongst thorn., (Applanse.) He stated that the proceeds of the gathering'werato be devoted towards the old folks treat fund,' and nothing would add,more to their .pleasitre,this Christmasiime than the feeling that they had been able to dd 'sbinething for thoSe -Wei were not in the isanie 'position us themselves:. (Applause.), • He then callodupon Mr. Legh to give ida lectnre., Mr. T. W. ,Legh, M.P.,' was Warmly received. He commenced by observing that Bulgaria., until recently. had )een a country little talked about or known, and when he expressed his intention of visiting that country he was asked what prompted him to do so and what was his Object in, going there. His reason was that for some time he had had quite sufficient of English or rather Irish politics,' and he WKS not averse to seeing ; another form of political agitation, and in the second place; he owned to a preference for -visiting those coun- tries, which lie out of the batten track of the ordinary tour. He gave a passing arzount of recent political events In Bulgaria, and proceeded to state that he commenced ihis tour at the end of August last, and his first impel-- taut stopping place was lielgrade; the capital of Servia. He next described the difficulties he met with in entering Bulgaria from Seriia, owing to the disturbed state of 'political affair:, and his subsequent drive to Sophia, the capital of Bulgaria, accompanied by the British Consul and the latter's wife. After commenting upon the dress. and customs of the people there, :he narrated a conver- sation he had with the Prince of Bulgaria, who he thought, occupied a most unenviable position, but was still &Serving every respect and recognition. He after- 'wards paid a visit to the monastery of San Rero, where what had been described as the Brigand adventure," becurred.: In reference to this matter he thought-The must consider himself a much ill-used person. The day following his arriyal at the monastery, he, in company with two ,gendarmes and two native hunters, decided to have a day's shooting; and with' that object journeyed for some hours in a magnificent forest. • During the day, ,and while they were going up a steep incline, he saw the gendarmes raise their rifles and point at unseen objects. Ho at that time was some distance behind them, and one of the native hunters came to and in- formed him that he had better prepare to defend himself as brigands were in the neighbourhood. Ho was requested to leave everything to the gendarmes as he did not know anything of the Bulgarian language and he did so. Directly afterwards he was informed that the gendarmes had stated he was an Englishman on a sport- ing expedition, and they *era allowed to depart in,peaae. He never intended to say anything about the incident, but ho was surprised to find a few hours afterwards that the monastery was visited by a company of militia, and he (Mr. Legh) and his friends were guarded and pro- tected in their subsequent movernents. He next referred to his' experiences during an election in Bulgaria, his visit to a prison in Sophia. and his return home along the Danube, and through Petth, Vienna, Sm. In com- menting upon the political aspect of Bulgaria, he said it was probable there would be serious struggles in • south eastern Europe, and ho thought the rule of the, Turks was bound to give place •to that of more vigorous nations: He thought if a strong and independent Bulgaria was created it would act as a song barrier against Russian aggression, and from motives of political, expediency, as well as justice and fair play, the cause of the Bulgarians should he sup- ported as much as possible. Any assistance they might give the Bulgarians would ,be to theinteract and beiefit of this country. (Applause.) 1 Mr. M. B. Westheati moved a. cordial vote of thanks to ' Mr. T. W. Legh, M.P., for his kindness in giving the lec- ture, and in doing so took the opportunity to wish him a very Merry Christmas 'and a happy ;Cow Year. (AP- plause.)--Colonel George McCorquodale, J.P., cordially seconded the motion, and congratulated those present in having amongst them a representative of the ancient house of Legh. (Applause.) The motion was enthusiastically passed, and Mr. Legh acknowledged the compliment. A programme of music was rendered by Mrs. Boys°, Mrs. Seton, and Mr. P. Hardie, who were warmly ap- plauded.

Softens water.— , , SUICIDAL EPIDEMIC.—An extraordinary epidemic of suicidal mania is occupying the Nottingham magistrates and the coroner this week. An elderly man tried to kill himself b,y jumping- over a precipice; a beggar twice attempted to destroy himself; and a young woman leapt into the river Trent, prompted, she said, by a vision. The girl has been dismissed., The others are under remand. Meanwhile a suicide has been accom- plished by a man cutting his throat through unfounded jealeuey of a paramour, his deceased wife's sister; and another hung himself with grief at his wife's death. P. H. White-Mel- ville," who said he had been a clegyman in Bloemfon- tein, The fracas took place that morning in a cab in which the aeferidant was 'driVitig the complainant to the office of the Superintendent of Police. March 14,

"Dear Fred,—You will be surprised at receiving a letter from nte, but, thank God, I am pleased to say I am getting better every day. I shall be so 'glad to breathe the fresh air again. It has seemed a dreadful long time to be in bed. You know I was taken to the hospital last April to be treated for Bright's Disease of the kidneys. Well, on July 31 they tapped me, and took away 304 ounces of water. The same thing was done again on September 18, and 408 ounces of water obtained. On • Oct. 9 I was discharged Isom the hos- pital as Incurable. In January this year (the 20th) was again tapped at home, and 360 ounces of water taken away. The St. Bartholomew's Hospital in London refused me admission as a hopeless case, and the St. Bartholomew's Hospital, Chatham, also refused me; as being the worst cake they had seen for years, and two local doctors gave me up as hopeless. When I came from the hospital it took three to put me to bed. My clothes had to be cut off. I was an Object of misery and despair. After the hospitals had refused me, and doctors given me op, my wife persuaded me to try HOP BITTERS,. and from the commencement have improved daily. I have only taken them seven weeks, and can now get downstairs and: walk about without even a stick. With the aid of a few snore bottles of the Bitters shall be well again. The water has left my body and legs. The only trace left is in my feet. It is a wonderful medicine. rwish I had tried it sooner, as I have nearly ruined myself and family with doctors' bills and other expenses. I might have been well long ago. At the hospital I had no appetite whatever, but since using the Bitters eat everything with a relish. The only difficulty is the expense; but must not mind that so long as I sun getting well. Are cheerful now that recovery is near, for every one had given me up as a bad job.—With best wishes to---.

FOR SEAMEN.—What is the difference between a I man at the mast-head of a ship and the ship itself? I The ship sails over the seas, mid the man sees over the sails. IT IS AN ILL FASHION THAT BENEFITS Nononv.—Big I buttons still continue to be very fashionable. A lady, missing two buttons from her dress, asked her little ' daughter if she had seen them. • "Yes, ma; the cook's got them. She uses them as lids to the saucepans." COMPLIMENT CAPPED.—When Sir Walter Scott met Manzoni, the latter said that he owed so much to the, Waverley Novels that his I Prontessi Sposi might be con- sidered Scott's ewn. To which Scott-replied, "In that case I Promes.9i Spot is my best novel." HE OMITTED THE B.—A German, being about to come to Ebgland. studied the language, and then said, I bought de Virar von Vakofield und a Vortbook, und I said, 'Vat for a lengvitch !' In two dais I read de Vicar von Vakefteld, und again I sal, 'Vat for a lengvitch !' Sot I come to Dover, und I ask a pottlesodvater, und no men know vat I mean," • THE CELT AT Larcoa.--Scene—Deck of Scotch steamer. Yessel is leaving Tighnabruaich. Cockney tourist to Celticsea,man : " Do you know if I can get luncheon on board ?" Celt: "She'll not know the per- son at all, at all." Cockney tourist: "You misunder- stand me, I think. What I asked was if I might get luncheon on board ?" Celt: " Ocb, yes, to be sure! She'll ferry likely come aboard at Tarbert." Cockney tourist gives it up. WHAT HE WaarrEn.—A certain fashionable Parisian Andy emphatically rules the roast. When literary ' "lions" dine with her, she gives each guest his turn to speak. One evening lately M. Henan was talking, when another guest ventured on some remark in an undertone. He was peremptorily silenced; but, when M. Henan had finished, the hostess touched the silver bell she keeps by her side, and said, "Now, sir, you can speak." "But, my dear madam," rejoined her guest, "I only wanted to ask for some more spinach !" Mrs. Gallup is an estimable lady whose hobby is house- decoration. One day last spring Mrs. Gallup was care- less enough to drink a glass of red ink, believing it to be claret. She was naturally alarmed when she discovered her mistake, but no harm came to her. The doctor who was summoned, upon hearing what had happened, drily remarked to her, "Mrs. Gallup, there is such a thing, you know, as pushing this rage for decorated interiors too far." At a public meeting a learned but very diffident gentleman was called upon to make a speech. Contrary to his own expectations and those of his friends, he made a remarkably brilliant speech, and at the dose of the meeting they crowded around him with words of praise and compliment. Among the number was his Irish ser- vant, a warm-hearted honest fellow, proud and fond of his master. Rushing forward with a glowing face, Pat cried out, " Ah, sor, ye did yerself proudly, sor! Shure an' I've always said, sor, that ye warn% such a fool as ye look, sor! Indade an yelre not." UNREASONABLE. •-•-• Recently a ranting Communist gathered a crowd and entertained them with his diatribes on the inequalities of riches and poterty. He was in the very midst of his fiery declarations that the capital of the rich belonged to the labouring classes, when a distinct voice -rose from the crowd— ‘:lreu've got a gold watch, and I haven't any. I want yours." The speaker was nonplussed, but at last he said—" I bought this watch and paid for it." "Don't make any difference," persisted the voice • "you've got a gold watch, and I haven't—l want it." The talker was checkmated, and the meeting broke up. A DOSE FOR a Docron.--The Hon. Sunset Cox was once visiting a physician in a thriving Ohio village which boasted the largest cemetery in that region. After dinner, while the coffee was being handed round, the host requested the witty Congressman to enrich his album with one of his humorous improvisations. "Cer- tainly," replied Cox, with a smile; and, drawing out his pencil, he wrote under the eyes of his entertainer the, following lines: "Stnce Dr. X. came to this town To cure diseases casual and hereditary, The hospital has been pulled down—" "Youfiatterer !" here exclaimed the doctor, mightily pleased; but the Congressman went on: "And they have made a larger cemetery." IN Luca. ANY WAY.—A story is told illustrative of the disadvantage of the houses in a terrace being too much alike. A man was asked to dinner, and he went to the house next door to the one to which he had been bidden. His name was announced, and the host stepped forward to welcome him. As it chanced, the guest knew the wife but not the husband. "I am so very Ibrry," said the host, "that my wife is too ill to come down-stairs. But we must get on as well as we can without her." Still thinking he was in the right house, the guest stayed on, took a pretty girl in to dinner, and had a charming evening. Two days afterwards he met the lady who was to have entertained him, and she as- sailed him with reproaches for spoiling the symmetry of her dinner-table, when it came out that he had inadver- tently dined next door. HE SootTLD HAVE TOLD me BOLL—There was once a very important state official in California who thought that everybody knew him or ought to know him. He was one day walking through a field, when a bull made for him With his head down and horns in a position to raise him. He was a state official, a man of dignity and political power and natural pomposity, but he ran. He ran surprisingly well. He ran even better than he did for office, and got to the fence first. He clambered over, out of breath and wanting dignity, and found the owner of the bull calmly contemplating the situation. -"What do you mean, sir,' asked the irate official, "by having an infuriated animal like that roaring over the fields ?" "Well, I guess the bull has some right in the field.' "Right—right! Do you know who I am, sir? Do you know who lam ?" The farmer shook his head. "I am General Blank, sir." "Then why, in thunder, didn't you tell the bull ?" asked the farmer. TRYING A RECIPE.—It was not until Mrs. Knaggee read the recipe in half-a-dozen different papers, that she concluded to give it a trial. We refer to that recipe, which says that "a table-spoonful of sawdust placed in each boot will keep the feet both dry and warm? The husband of Mrs. Knaggee was always complaining about cold feet, and so the other morning she poured two table- spoonfuls of sawdust into his boots. The result rather surprised her. He slipped on hi a boots, atehis breakfast,, and started for his place of business. He had not gone twenty-five yards from the house before he retraced his steps, and commenced to orate on profane history. As soon as he got into the dining-room he assisted one boot off with the toe of the other, and kicked it against a two- pun-ten mirror, while its mate struck his seven-year-old son on the head, and made him yell lustily.

_ "A WOLF IN SHEEP'S CLOTHING." Sir,—lii a publication now being widely circulated as the "Magazine of Fashion," I find amongst the follies of fashionable inanities a most deleterious piece of informa- tion, viz., the virtues of herbs—thus, we are told that "A decoction of this herb (Foxglove), mixed with honey, will purge and clean.se the body," /cc. Now, in this there is not a word to warn the reader that the plant foxglove is a virulent poison and must only be dealt with under great preeaution, and that with the supervision of a qualified medical man. Again, nothing is said as to the dose—it may be anything, from a handful upwards. Now, sir, had the publisher contented hitriself with dealing with his specialty nothing need to said about it, whatever we may think. It is only when he leaves this and incautiously gives medical advice, and that neither sound nor safe, that the public need to be warned against his nostrums. The scientific accuracy of the rest may be gauged by the fact that fumitory is recommepded as a depilatory on the authority of Di scoriele-q , whoever ' he may have been. And we are told that "hemlock resembles parsley," which it does'in one respect—they are both plants, and none but a fool would mistake the one for the other, while the fool's-parsley is so much nearer in appearance to the garnishing herb.—l am Sir, yours. Sic., JOHN PEERS. Penketh, 21st Dec., 188.

THE NATIONAL PROHIBITION PARTY. Sir,—lt is now coming to be generally recognised that "it is as much a Christian man's duty to take an active part in public life as it is to say his prayers." The old orthodoxy which viewed man almost exclusively from a spiritual standpoint is now giving way to a more rational view of his nature—that not only has he a soul to be saved, but a body with varied needs and necessi- ties. There is no reason why we should shrink from the logic of facts. The Liquor Trade is embrutalizing and pauperizing the people ; it is the fruitful source of crime, insanity, poverty, and untold sin and misery ; and yet, strange to say, our efforts up to the present have been largely directed to the tinkering/ up of 'these evils. This mode of proceeding cannot, go on Much 'longer. We must deal with causes, and this is the aim of the National Prohibition Party, which seeks "to secure the suppression of the liquor traffic by the direct and drastic remedy of Imperial enactment." Is the liquor trade right or wrong? What are its chief results ? Transference of wealth to the few, lasting misery of the many. It is the curse of our nation; it is subversive of man's highest in- terests; it is opposed to the Kingdom of God, and we have every reason to believe that, if Jesus Christ were with us again in the flesh, he would sternly denounce those men who legalize and uphold this infamous traffic. Right or wrong? That is the question. ",The first of all Gospels is this, that a lie cannot endure for ever."— Yours truly, • AA IV. H. BUTLER, Dec. 21, 1887. Grosvenor Terrace, Latchford.

WARRINGTON GAS ACCOUNTS. Sir,—l left at your office a day or two ago a copy of the Gem World, and shall be glad if you will give a fr'l copy of the editor's remarks on the accounts said to be Warrington Corporation gas accounts; but my opinion is the heading is wrong, and should be the accounts of a private committee, of which Mr. Merman Holmes is the chairman. For some seven or eight years I havg applied to various gentlemen to examine the accounts and give me a. repo.... One and all have had one reoort, which was that the accounts were so confused that, without more information was given, nothing cord be made of them. To the above I had one exception; the gentleman was a public auditor, and when be had spent five or six hours over the copy I lent him, he returned it. and said the accounts Were so perfectly confused that the gentleman who had made them up should have somii honour conferred on him for the work done. I think the present report does not differ very much indqed from the former ones. Some of the gentlemen whom I did apply to inquired what the particulars were that I wanted. My first question was, why were the accounts confused? The second was, to what extent were they confused? and the third was, what was tse object of haying them confused? I may say nearly all gave me answer, and the differences in them were not much. When the report has been read I hope some steps will be taken to have the accounts put in such a form that they can be brought before the Town Council, which has not been done for many years. I should like to remind the public that when a copy of the last accounts was laid on the table of the Council chamber, Mr. Cour clilor Bolton inquired of the chairman of the Gas Committee if the accounts could be discussed. The reply was that they could not, and that the only time for discussion was when the estimates were made. As the Gas Com- mittee never make any estimates, the question is, when will the committee put their accounts befor e he Council ?—Yours truly, FRANCIS DIXON. Arplev-street. Warrington, Dec. 14, 1887. EXTRACT FROM THE "GAS WORLD." The following is an extract from the editorial referred to in the "Gas World" of 10th December, 1887: ' The gas amounts of the Warrington and Doncaster Corporations furnish examples of the confusion to which we have referred. These accounts are correct in the same way as the Army and Navy Estimates are correct. The accounts are correct; but the information to be ob- tained from them is very limited, and the little that is to be got costs some considerable study. Were it not for a little table, furnished by the gas engineer, Mr. James Paterson, the Warrington accounts would yield none of that information which the intelligent student of gas accounts looks for. "Balance, being profits," is, no doubt, pleasing to the eye; but " balanne being profits made in the manner fully specified above" conveys more information to the student—be he a councillor, a rate- payer, or a unit of the general public. After what we have just said, it is scarcely necessary to state that the Warrington accounts do not admit of an analysis in the tabular form. Here, then, we NN:11 attempt to bring a little order out of tlie chaos before us. From Mr. Paterson's table we learn that the quantity of coal carbonized during the year ended the 25th March last was 20,858 tons; and that this yielded 200.933,700 cubic feet of gas, or at the rate of 9.632 cubic feet per ton. These quantities are respectively 5'4 and 4.3 per cent, above those of the previous year. The sales, how- ever, are much less satisfactory. Although the quantity of gas made has increased by 4.3 per cent., the quantity sold and accounted for has decreased by about 6 per cent. How Warrington happens to have a leakage of 14 per cent, we cannot say; but the accounts give this figure. A few of the more interesting items in Mr. Paterson's table we will give without comment : Capital in works and plant, £178,181, 14s. 10(1. ; capital per ton of coal, £8 Us. 9d.; capital per million cubic! feet of gas. £BB6 9s. 6d.; capital per £lOO of gas rental, £OO2 Is. 3d.; gas rental per £lOO of capital, £l6 11s. 3d.; , gas rental per £lOO expended in coal and cannel, £294' ! les.; gas rental per mile of mains, £627 145.; gas dis- tributed per mile of main, 5,021,460 cubic feet. Another point of interest in this table is that the rental received per thousand cubic feet of gas sold last year was 2.5. 11d., whereas for the previous year it was only 2s. Bd. The rates for the two periods appear to have been the same; therefore, the difference must be due to a reduction in bad debts or in a more limited application of the scale of discounts. The revenue account shows a total income of £40,178, 10d„ and after providing for all revenue charges a balance of £11,844 Os. ma. remains, being: equal to about 7 per cent, per annum on the total capital invested in the undertakinci As affecting this point, we may men- tion that the price charged for the 18-candle gas supplied ranges from 2s. 6d. to 3s. ner thousand cubic feet. Prom this grog profit a sum of £10,205 6s. falls to be deducted for interest, annuities, and redemption of debt, leaving a net surplus of £1,638 14s. 71d. Adding this to the surplus of previous years, and deducting £99 17s. 7d. transferred to capital, we have a balance of £13,432 19s. 30. The gasworks are utterly devoid of anything of the nature of a reserve fund; in fact, the policy pursued seems to be one of a very hand-to-mouth description.

FRODSHAM. FRODSV \M MUSICAL SOCIZTY.—The first concert of the season was held in the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Tues- day evening. There was a fair attendance. The first part or the programme was devoted to Dr. Stainer's ora- torio "The daughter of Jairus," the choruses of which were rendered by the members of the society, numbering upwards of thirty voices, under the conductorship of Mr J. R. Curnow, of Chester. Mr. Charles Hibbert, of Frodsham, presided at the pianoforte, and the Rev. Hor- ace Stephens, rector of Handley, Cheshire, at the har- monium. The principals were Miss Louie Richardson (soprano), Mr. Levison Myatt, of Chester Cathedral (tenor), and the Rev. R. Nunn, vicar of Norley (bass.) The second part of the programme consisted of a miscel- laneous selection of vocal and instrumental mus'c. ii the choruses were sung with great care and taste through. out, showing excellent training, and reflected great credit upon the conductor (Mr. Curnow.) The proceed- ings were brought to a close by the singing of the Na- tion .1 A nthem . THE PROJECTED BRANCH LINE FROM TATTENHALL ROAD TO HALTON.—On Thursday evening week a meetint, of the parishioners of Kingsley and Newton was held in the Girls' Schoolroom, Kingsley. The Vicar (Rev. A. P. Reynolds), who presided, in the course of a few opening remarks, referred to the considerable inconvenience experienced by many of the farmers and tradesmen in in this and the adjoining neighbourhood owing to the I want of more convenient railway accommodation. The Chairman then called upon Mr. Joseph Hail, of Kings- wood, to address the meeting. Mr. Hall said it would, in his opinion. be a great benefit to the neighbourhood if the directors if the London and North-Wes:ern Railway Company could be prevailed upon to make the junction of the proposed railway from Tattenhall-road at Halton instead of at Helsby, as in the latter case it would pass through a district where there was but little need for such accommodation. After a little more discussion it was unanimously resolved, "That a committee be formed at ,Kingsley to act conjointly with the one at Tarvin, for the purpose of gathering information, and also to petition the before-mentioned company to have a station at Kingsley." The members of the Board Were put to con-, siderable inconvenience in consequence of the boardroom having been utilised since the previous meeting as a hospital, consequent upon the over-crowded nature of the workhouse hospital. T. Operations in connection with the ConstructiOn o' the Ship Canal commenced at Eastham—the point where the canal wajoin the Mersey—on the 11th ult.,and work has since been started at various poipta on the route, and the construction a the large dock at the Salford end of the canal has now been com-' raenced. The site of the dock is the extensivi plot of land known as the Mile which lies between Trafford-road and the Racecourse. Here a number of men are at work excavating the soil and m4king other preparations necessary to the carrying out et the great undertaking. The land was formerlfr the property of Lord Egerton, of Tatton (the chairman of the Ship Canal Company), and seeing that it did not come into the possession of the company until last week it is evident that no time has been lost by the contractor (Mr. Walker) in commencing active operations. there: Owing to the fact that the place is aconsiderable distance from any rail vvay station some inconvenience is being experienced in gettitp on to the ground the n ecessaty Plant and material, the bulk of which will, it is believed, be broughtrby barges from Runcorn. Already several consign- ments of timber have reached the spot, and morei are to follow. Of course the news that work had been begun at the Salford. end of 'the canal soon snread in the vicinity, the Consequence being that' Mr. L. P. Nott, the agent of the' section lying be- tween Salford and Barton, very soon had tO deal with numerous applicants for employment. It Was found impossible to find work for them, at once. Until additional plant is on the ground, and mat- ters have reached a more advanced stage. no large amount of labour can be usefully employed ; it is, however, expected that when the Christmas and New Year holidays are over work will be found for two or three lsundred labourers. Perhaps the best way of giving an idea of the amount of labour which will eventually.be required in the construc- tion of the dock is to give its dimensions. The water area of the dock which is to be 26ft. deep, will be about 254, acres, and the available leiwth of quay frontage is equal -to 1•17 imile It may be added that good roads will be made from the dock to the adjacent roads and streets, and that on the quart there will be teansit sheds, with hydraulic machinery and crapes suitable for the rapid hand- ling of large cargoes. The prolonged unfavourable weather has consi- derably retarded the work rastham. Mr. Manisty, the contractor's agent, is '..indated with applica- tions for emnloyment, hut, for the reason stated, he has refrained from increasing the number of work- men, which now stands at 800. The railway which runs alongside the canal line is constructed as far as Poole Hall, and is now 2i miles in length, the materials and machinery are being sent to the front with great rapidity, and, weather permitting: all will he in readiness at the commencement of the year for a good start to be made in connection with the cutting of the canal, and work will also be pro- vided for a large number of additional hands. Two steam navvies are constantly at work at Eastham. where a tug and flats have been added to the machinery for facilitating the work. Workmen, are nowl busily engaged in laying a temporary railway at Rixton, behind the New Hall. The two locomotive engines, the " Mersey " and '!lrvvell," have been conveyed by road from Irlam station, and also a steam navvy. Every preparation is being made to commence in earnest. 'Timber, metals, &e., are arriving by the river in large quantities.- and a yard or depot has been made called Pool's Dock, near Hollins Green. The rail- way is to extend along the course 'of the canal to Irlam, where preparations are in active progress for a siding out of the Cheshire Lim Railvay to the east of Irlam Station. Another large number of tip waggons have ,ar- rived at Latchford station, where the specially constructed siding in now in full use. The mate- rial brouTht to Latchford station. where it is con- stantly arriving, is rapidly transferred by, means of the siding to barges on the canal, by Whi6h means it is conveyed to its dest:nation. ,Scrne loco- motives are daily expected.. The 'work at Acton Orange continues to be pushed forward as rapidly as possible. ,

div.head: WARRINGTON SCHOOL OF ART.
div.p: WARRINGTON SCHOOL OF ART.

EXHIBITION OF STUDENTS' DRAWINGS. On Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday of the pre- sent week the School of Art in Museum-street has been thrown open to the public in order that they might witness an exhibition of the drawings and other work which has been done by the students between July of last year and July of this year. In the course of those three days the school has been visited by a very large number of the inhabitants of the town who have thus had an opportunity of seeing and judging for themselves of the work that" is being done there. The exhibition was one of great variety, and many of the drawiags, paintings, and moilellin2s that were to be seen were of much merit in- deed, and justly entitle Mr. Barkas,the headmaster (who is ably assisted by Mr. Aylward, second master, and other assistants), as well as the students themselves, to very high praise. The quantity of the work done at the School of Ai;:, may be to some extent guaged by the fact that the four rooms in which the drawings, &c., were hung, were filled to repletion, and the space afforded in the vestibule and staircase was also fully utilised. The room to the right on entering the School is the architectural and mechanical room, and here we find some excellent studies of machine and building cow ic- tion, architectural drawings, and examples of plane and solid geometry. These for the most part are the work of yourr, persons actively entraeed in mechanical occu- pations of one kind or another, and who must have de- rived some very useful technical knowledge from their • connection With the school. It would be Im- possible to pafticularise to any extent, but amongst drawings of a commendable character were one of the sections of a Mansard roof by Mr. A. Downe, and some of machine and building construction by J. H. Smethurst and J. C. Dewhurst respectively. In this room there were also to bo seen some details of classic archi- tecture admirably draw nby Hollins Allen. One side of the adjacont large elementary room was taken up as*th various decorative designs for textiles, wall papers. &c. An exceedingly tasteful example of ornamental etching on glass vaisels was likewise on view, the artist being W. E. Ray. The student (P. Hill), who has obtained a Queen's pi*ze for a wall decoration exhibits some of his work, which is harmonious and pleasing in colouring, and the ornamentation is well distributed, and NCI, when completed, no doubt look very handsome. G. Hoelt shows two excellent examples of stencilling, one of which represents the work in process and the other the finished result. Another piece of stencilling—a panel—by W. Hobson, was also desm Mg of mention. A desi•Yn for a stained glass fanlight window by W. G. Knight attracted a good deal of attention, being hold and igorous in conception and rich in colour. There were corms studies of plants, which had been --st of all pm rayed from nature and afterwards conventionalised to fi" variously shaped spaces, and in this connection we may mention Miss A. Cht;mes and Hollins Aliens; while J. A. Bunch and J. Evans contribute careful sttees of Oifferent styles of ornament. The large element-11y room was, however, chiefly furnished with specimens of the. earlier -stages of drawings, including outlines from the fiat, shading from the cast, and shad- ing of groups and models. Several very creditable out- lines from the fiat were exhibited by H. Plumpton. H. Pierpoint, and D. Stone, and a number of others. With reference to the shading from the cast we might mention H. A. Barkas, A. Gleave, V. Fleming., G. P. Williamson, and J. Ray. Some very promising samples of water- colour draw'ngs had been contributed by Miss L. Flet- cher, Miss Robinson, Miss Shipton, Miss aldwell. Miss Finley, and Miss Walton. In the hall of the school were to be seen praiseworthy drawings by Miss L. Dutton. a study of pigeons and shading from the case by Mew V'

The galrdipl- League, by its ramifications, had made itself so power- ful that no poor man dare disol ey it. • The government however, came to the help of the oppreased, and deir mined to relieve the Wish peasant from the miseries of being boycotted. The government also ve.; properly de- terminel that the National Leaguers should not hold meetims at which to propagate their despicable, mean, wicked and abominable doctrines. They had now, in power a government ready; able, and willing to put dos. n disorder in Ireland, and the question was would they support that goveinment 'He had no. doubt that they world. They would prevent the National. League from doing any more mischief, and would let the Irish peasant enjoy his liberty. Then capital and confidence would return ta Irelapd, and the people of that country would become happy, contented; and law-abiding.

div.head: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER.
div.p: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER.
[FROM OUR OWN CORRESPONDENT.] 23, Old Broad-stnet, E.C.

_ There has been a marked coni,rast this week in the financial world with the preceding week. Up to Satur- day everything was "booming," and the word rag passed round to buy ,everything with the consequence that prices wenz up all round, With the commencentent of the week quite a different aspect was presented, and the contrast was all the greater by its soddenness. • CM the Stock Exchange transactions have narrowed down to the smallest limits, and by the imc this letter appears business until after the Christmas holidays will be practically over as the house closes until the folloWlng Tuesdty, when the Last settlement of the year com- mences. Investors will be wise perhaps to do nothing until the turn of the year 4 at any rate they should not sell, as the present prices-in money Stocks are lower than they have bsen.for a few weeks, and with-the turn of the year a renewed upward movement may be fully anticipated.. Home rails which 'rose all round last week show rou- siderable decline now, and they are certainly Worth buying at the present prices, carrying, as they th 4 the half-yearly dividend. Brighton A's especially are worth an ezrly purchase. • • ' One of the most extraordinary rushes of new com- panies was made last Saturday by the promoters:' -ne lest; than a dozen coMpanies, with a captal of over four millions, soddenly came out; but the result was that the whole thing was entirely overdone, and on Monday more than half had retired fro n the field. So little, in- deed, was the chance of the best of them getting their money, that the promoters were obliged to withdraw and pocket the loss already incurred. . Investors cannot be too careful in going into new un- dertakings just 110 W, as every promoter who has a pros- pectus is anxious to bring it out before the passing of the Governmeutbill to amend the Companies' Acts. The absolute need for limn() such measure in the interests of the public has long. been recognised, and until it is passed investors should look with more than usual su.s- picion on all undertakings. • ' Mining companies stiil hold their position, with the exception of copper, which has had a fall during this week. Rio Tinto's, as the representative of these corn. panies, last week went to 23, but have since fallen to 20. Gold mining companies, especially South Afeican, con- tinue strong. ' Moodie's,. with 7s del paid, are! £3. In other similar companies, Don Pedro's have during the past few weeks 'gone fromlla to Xs, with the proba- bility of their reaching doutire" this. price. Foreigners are quite beyond the reach of ordinary, prediction, and investors, who_object to have their peace of :mind dbturbed, and their stra mide , the dice of English and foreign soeculators, would a, well to get rid of these without delay. • In the American market priecs` still continue flat, but, there are several investments in rails deserving of a purchase at present prices, as a jump in Americans at any moment is quite within the bounds of prebabilitT

Baron Dowse, of the Irish bench, is'very ill. Mr. Sext3n, M.P., Fes seriously ill at his: Dublin n i isi- dence. His iPress s stated to be of a.typhoid nature, The Speaker, in Frilly night's ",Gazette," notifies his intention dissaing, six days hence, a new writ for Winchester.
• Lord Hai Lington left town last night for Kimbolton Castle, where he will spend the Christmas holidays as guest of the Duke of Manchester.

FIREIN DUBLIN.—On Friday morning the work- shops aad storerooms of Messrs. Martin, of Stephen's Green, Dublin, were destroyed by fire. The Mansion House was in great danger, but was saved owing to the praiseworthy efloits of the fire brigade. BURNED TO DEATIL—At Leicester, On Friday, a wontan named Priest, wife of a coal dealer living in Waring- street, was burnt ,o death; ' She got up between four and five o'clock to do some ironing, and is supposed to have been seized with a fit in which she knocked a paraffin lamp over. • FATAL ACCIDENT TO AN ENGINE DRIVER.—INVO engine cl-ivers in the employ of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Reway Company were crossing the line to, proceed to their work, at Accrington, on Friday forenoon, when they were knocked down by a passenger train. One of them named Fielding, was killed, and the other seriously injured. fIINERAL OF TF‘ll LATE REV. A. IL MACRONOCRIE. —The funeral of the Rev. A. H. Machanochie took place on Friday at Woking, in presence of a large number of people. A set lee was performed previously at St.Albans, Holooin, with much ritual ceremony, and a procession of clergy in surplices accompanied the corpse through the streets to Waterloo Station. ,

COLLISION TN THE AttRSEY.—ASeri.OUSCOMMOROCCUT"EI. in the Mensey early on Friday morning,. The Spanish steamer Roclas, inward buund from Seville, and the Ca.spopedia, outward,' bound for China collided with such force that the former sank in a short time. The crew were saved .by a tug boat. The tother colliding steamer was considerably damaged, and came to an anchor in the river. HUNTING IN IRELAND.—Speakiug at a Prinirose League meeting held at Hull on Friday afternoon, Lord Harris referred at some length to the action recently taken by certain landlords in County Meath in yielding to menaces in order to be allowed to continue. hunting. Such conduct, in •hi s lordship's opinion' was calcidated to strike a harder blow at the Union than could ever ne given by the National League. - . FATAL COLLIERY ACCIDENT.—OO Friday morning John: Howarth, aged 29, of Peel-s.reet, .Rochdale, was., killed in Butterworth Hall Colliery, Milhrow. BIB° he was following his employment as a col'ier about a. ton of earth and stone 'fell Ironi the roof upon the poor fellow., His fellow workmen set at once to release him, but it took half an hour to remove the fallen debris, and it was then found that he was dead. • VESSEL ON FruN.—While the barge, Lighter A'rov' ince, of Newcastle, was being towed; on Friday,', from the Tyne to. Middlesborough,laden with barrels ot.Petroleutr4 the oil somehow took fire off•the mouth of Shields Harbour. The flames spread with terrible rapidity, and the crew had barely time to escaPe by taking a small boat, 'from which they were picked up and landed at North Shields. The vessel and cargo were entirely destroyed. FATAL AFFRAY Loug,hrea correspon- dent Aays that as two young men named Ylannion and Dwyer, were returning from .Loughrea to Kilreecle, on Thursday night, an'altercation took place between them, during which, it is aAleged,.Dwyer fatally. stabbed Man- nion, and afterwards gave himself •up to the, police at Kißeecle.e- rite cause of. the alleged murder is at present Unknown, 'but 'an „Ruttiest will be: held; pending which Dwyer is detained in- custody. • : ,

div.head: W,II'tIUNGTON SAVINGS BANK.
div.p: W,II'tIUNGTON SAVINGS BANK.

The annual meeting in connection With this bank was held Ott Tuesdav,intheßank Buildings, Butter- market-street. Alderman Pickmere,, chairman of the managers, presided, and there were also .preseiit Mr. W. Long (vice-chairman), the .Mayer (Alderman. Sutton), Aldermen Harrison, Davies, and ;Webster ; and Messrs. T. Jolley, F. Monks. R. Garnett. Litton, J. R. Young; H. N. Horton, James Morris, . Win. Derbyshire, F. W. Monks. T. E. Withington, and J. R. Davies (actuary.) The ACTUARY read the annual report and the . statement of accounts, from which it appeared that the total funds amounted to £298,248 Os 10d, there being a balance with the treasurer of £2.878 us. The total amount due to depositors was £293,958 us 3d. leaving a surplus of £2,291 9s 7d. The sums of £7,727 Us 5d interest, and £l9l 17s dividends on stock,- had. been credited depositors, and the total anoint due to them showed an increase for thaiFear of £5lB 13s Bd. There had been 803 new accounts opened, and 809 accounts had been closed, showing an increase for the year of 194, the total • pu,mber of depositors now being 9,778. The stock register showed a balance of , £7,275 of £3 per cent. eensols., The 15,342 transactions during the year showed that the bank ,was doing well, and it WAS very satisfactory in these times to report a general increase in accounts and money: The usefulness of the irstitetion could not be denied, and now that the bank was open daily, every facility and encouragement was given to those who wished to be provident.—The CHAIR3fAN proposed the adoption of the report, and in doing so said that thwas the eveptleth annual meet- ing of the bank. He remembered that in his youth the institution was a very' different one to what it was now. It was formerly situated in Bank-street. in a snAll room, there was one clerk, and it was open for a couple of hours on Wednesdays and Saturdays. Now they had nearly £300,000 deposited, and almost 10,000 depositors. One of their old clerks. Mr. Lomas, had retired, and, he had been presented with a gratuity of £lOO out of the surplus. The number of transactions this year had in- creased by about 300, and -the amount deposited by about £soo.—The proposition'thua moved by the Chair- Man, was seconded by Mr. W. LONG, who expressed his confidence that the bank was doing a good work. and said that the later meetings that the committee had held had given signs of that improvement in thrift that they as 'supporters of the bank hoped for.—The MAYOR re- marked that he thought it very satisfa,ctory that there were nearly 10.000 depositors out of a population of something like 40.000. It spoke well for the town.—The CHORMAN therenpan remarked that, .Warrington, in the number of depositors in proportion to its population, I stood fifth in all Lancashire, the others being Manches- ter, Liverpool, Preston, and Blackburn. The statement of accounts was then adopted.—Mr. R. GARNETT pro- pmecl the adoption of the report of the Committee of Management, embodying with Ids resolution a vote of thanks to the gentlemen acting on the committee for their valuable F.PTViCCS during the past year. The 3notion was seconded by Mr. 11. J. Homes:, and carrited.—On' the proposition of .Mr. Mowasf seconded by Mr. T. Jourrir. Alderman Pickmere Was re-elected Chairman. and Mr. W. Long vice-chairman—On the motion of Captain WITHINOTON, seconded by Mr. F. W. MONKS, the following gentlemen were appointed to serve on the Committee of Management :—The chairman and vice- chairman, and Messrs. F. Monks, S. Rigby, T. Litton, and J. Davies (trustees) ; and the Mayor (Alderman Sut- ton), Messrs. T. Jolley, W. Darbyshire, W. Owen, J. R. Young, J. Morris, Joseph Harrison, and the Rev. John 'Vonge (managers).—The CHAIRMAN referred to the loss sustained by the death during the year of four of the trustees—Messrs. Peter Bylands, M.P., George Crosfield, Charles Broadbent; and Captain Reynolds—and it was then resolved that the following gentlemen be elected trustees :—Messrs. James Tinsley, George Dakin, John Geddes, R. Garnett, and T. Jolley.—Mr. R. GARNETT said that he had seen so much of the importance of thrift that he did not think too much could be said upon the question. It' had occurred to him that while they had such a large amount of surplus they might make an offer of £2O for an essay on the subject, confined to competi- tors' in Warrington and the neighbourhood, the essay to be afterwards printed and circulated with a If lew to in- creasing the number of depositors. This suggestion at once met with anproval, and it was decided to recom- mend the Committee of Management to adopt it.—Votes of thanks to the chairman and vice-chairman brought the proceedings to a close.

PRESENTATION AT IRELETH &MK/L.—A large number of friends and scholars attended at the Ire- leth School on Saturday. to witness the presenta- tion of a testimonial to Miss Cooper, on her leaving Ireleth for Livernool. The testimonial consisted of "The Casquet of literature," splendidly bound, in three vols., and a beautiful glove and handkerchief box. In each of the volumes and on the box was an illuminated address as follows Presented to Mies Cooper (on her resigning the post Of schoolmis- tress at the Ireleth Church of England School) by her scholars and a few friends as an ackpowledgment of the many kind and courteous acts received at her hands during the last three years." The presents- tion,was made by the Vifar, the Rev. T. Douglas. Miss Cooper is a daughter of Mr. Edmund C. Cooper, of Winwick. • _ _

FRIENDS' SCHOOL, PENKETH.—On Tuesday even- ing the Christmas entertainment was 'given by the scholars of the Friends' School. Penketh, in the lec- ture hall of the school, which had been nicely decorated. There was a large audience present. A favourable report as to the work of the school dur- ing the past year was read by Mr. J. T. Gumersall, the head-master, after which prizes to successful scholars were distributed by Mr. Holmes. On the proposition of Mr. W. E. Turner. a hearty vote of thanks was accorded Mr. and Mrs Gumersall. In the entertainment a 'scene from the "Merchant of Venice" was rendered by six girls, the part of Por- tia being taken by Miss S. M. Haworth. Songs. instrumental selections, recitations. &e. were after- wards rendered by Miss Haworth, Miss Caulfield, Messrs. James Charnock. Davies. Woolman, Gibbs; and H. Newhouse. The programme likewise inclu- ded a scene from the" Pickwick Papers," and a song, "The ghost of a Penketh scholar," by Mrs Gumer- sail. A very enjoyable entertainment was brought to a close shortly ,before ten o'clock.

" CHRTSTMA S CAROLS."

At a "popular service" held at Wycliffe Congre- - gational Church, Warrington, on Sunday evening, the Rev. John Yonge gave an address to a large congregation on the subject of "Christmas Carols." Referring to the approaching Christmas time, the reverend gentleman said that besides the great mul- titude who hailed .Chrristmas with pleasure, there - was another multitude who had rather forget than remember it, We had come to think of Christmas - as a world-wide festival, and in one sense it was, and yet it was also the fact that, either through poverty or sorrow, there were many who had neither' the means nor the heart to join in its festivity. Human experiences, whether of prosperity or ad- versity, of gladness or of sorrow, were accentuated by a time like Christmas, and the heart that could. refuse to enter into its joyfulness, would be likely to sink the deeper in sorrow and despondency. His subject that evening led him to deal with Christmas as a time of song, of joy, and of festivity, but each Christmas that canie seemed to bring more power- fully to his mind the other side—the darker and • sadder side—on which, by force of circumstances, . so many were compelled to sit. He could not ignore the sadder side of Christmas, and so he would begin his address by venturing an appeal. There were • families known to him, and to his colleague at • • Cockheelge mission, to whord this Christinas time would bring little or no cheer at all, unless some- how either they or he could send it them. He asked those who could afford to do so to • render these families some assistance, either by sending to him privately any gift dating the week or dropping a 'contribution into the offertory boxes, at the door. Let them be assured that that practi- cal kind of sympathy was not only calculated to • rouse gladness in the hearts of those who might be ' benefitted by it, but would be acceptable to Hird I who was the Lord of this annual festival, who was its author as well as its giver. Proceeding, Mr. Yonge said that the Christmas carol WtLi a very old institution, coming down to us from very primitive times. Therefore it was a subject with which they should be disposed to deal. tenderly. The custom could be traced back distinctly to the very early days of the English Church, and early English carols were sung partly in Latin and parbly in the mother tongue. Many of them partook of the na- ture of historical ballads, and many were founded upon legends which were interesting now-a-days, only as showing the exceeding simplicity of the people of the by-gone days. Having spoken further on his subject, and given instances of carols, Mr. Yonge told his hearers thatunless they opened their hearts tO the Saviour, and admitted Him, they Could know nothing of real Christmas joy. Let this Christmas time be the advent 'of His entrance to their hearts. After,the address, which was listened to with marked attention, Miss Nellie Roberti sans "Room for thee." ' ' •
